Selects the built-in compaction strategy GridLayout uses via its compactType prop.

Lives in `keystone-dashboard-layout-core`, not this package's own
barrel — a real (value) export there, so you can both type
`compactType` and compare/construct against these at runtime:

```ts
import { ECompactType } from 'keystone-dashboard-layout-core';
```

```ts
enum ECompactType {
  NONE = 'none',
  HORIZONTAL = 'horizontal',
  HORIZONTAL_OVERLAP = 'horizontal-overlap',
  VERTICAL = 'vertical',
  VERTICAL_OVERLAP = 'vertical-overlap',
}
```

| Value | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `NONE` | No compaction at all — items stay exactly where placed, gaps included. Colliding items still get pushed down out of the way; this is distinct from `VERTICAL_OVERLAP` below — turning compaction off has never meant turning collision resolution off too. |
| `HORIZONTAL` | Items compact leftward, floating to the smallest available `x` without colliding with anything already placed. |
| `HORIZONTAL_OVERLAP` | Horizontal compaction, but every non-static item moves straight to `x: 0` unconditionally, ignoring collisions entirely — matching `react-grid-layout`'s own `allowOverlap` semantics applied to compaction specifically. Items may end up visually overlapping as a result. |
| `VERTICAL` (default) | Items compact upward, floating to the smallest available `y` without colliding with anything already placed. |
| `VERTICAL_OVERLAP` | Vertical compaction, but every non-static item moves straight to `y: 0` unconditionally, ignoring collisions. Same overlap semantics as `HORIZONTAL_OVERLAP`, applied to the vertical axis. |

Replaces an older, separate `verticalCompact: boolean` prop — a single
enum-valued prop is easier to extend (the two `*_OVERLAP` members add a
capability the boolean couldn't express at all) and easier to reason
about than a growing pile of independent booleans.

See [Pluggable compaction](/react/api/interfaces/compactor/) for the
`compactor` prop that lets you replace the algorithm entirely instead
of picking one of these five, and [Pluggable compaction (compactType &
compactor)](/react/examples/pluggable-compaction/) for a live demo
switching between all five plus a custom compactor.
What keyboard and screen-reader support Keystone Dashboard Layout for Angular actually provides — and what it deliberately doesn't (yet).

Same scope and reasoning as the Vue port's own
[Accessibility scope](/vue/guide/project/accessibility/) — this page
documents this package's own implementation specifically, confirmed
directly against `grid-item.component.ts`'s own source.

## What's implemented

### Keyboard move and resize

Every non-static, editable `GridItemComponent` is keyboard-focusable
(`[attr.tabindex]` resolves `0`) and operable:

- **Arrow keys** move it by one grid unit, if it's draggable.
- **Shift + arrow keys** resize it by one grid unit, if it's resizable.

Each keypress is treated as a complete, atomic gesture — `handleKeydown`
emits a synthetic `dragstart` immediately followed by `dragend` (or
`resizestart`/`resizeend`) via the eventBus, the same two calls a real
mouse gesture's start and release would produce, so
`GridLayoutComponent`'s own compaction/collision/`multiSelect`
group-move handling applies identically regardless of which input
method triggered the change. This two-call shape (not just a single
synthetic `dragend`) is a real, confirmed fix in this port's own
history — an earlier version emitted only `dragend`, which meant a
keyboard-driven move of a selected item never brought the rest of the
`multiSelect` selection along with it, since the group-move snapshot is
taken at `dragstart` specifically.

**Works with `multiSelect`'s group move/resize too** — see
[Multi-select & group move/resize](/angular/features/) for the feature
overview.

**Deliberately scoped to single-unit steps**, not a full
[WAI-ARIA grid](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/grid/) or
[application](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/) widget pattern.
This library isn't a traditional data grid — it's a freeform draggable
canvas — so the full APG grid pattern doesn't map cleanly onto it.

### Screen reader support

- Each interactive item gets `role="group"` and
  `aria-roledescription` (default `"Draggable, resizable item"`), so a
  screen reader announces it as something other than a plain, silent
  `<div>`.
- `aria-describedby` points to a visually-hidden instructions string
  ("Press arrow keys to move." / "Press shift plus arrow keys to
  resize.", each only included if that action actually applies to the
  item) — discoverable on focus, not a mandatory upfront announcement.
- A visible focus outline, so a keyboard user can actually see which
  item currently has focus.

A real, confirmed gap existed here until this was implemented: despite
`GridLayoutComponent`'s own `scrollToItem`/`focusItem` doc comments
already claiming items "get `tabindex='0'` via `GridItemComponent`'s
own host bindings," no `tabindex` binding of any kind existed on this
component beforehand — confirmed via a direct grep turning up zero
matches. `focusItem()` calling `.focus()` on a genuinely non-focusable
element was a real, silent no-op in any actual browser.

### A deliberate, non-obvious design decision worth calling out

Keyboard move/resize **ignores `dragAllowFrom`/`dragIgnoreFrom`/
`resizeIgnoreFrom`** entirely — `handleKeydown` reads only
`resolvedIsDraggable`/`resolvedIsResizable` and never touches any of
the three. Those fields restrict which DOM element a *mouse* drag/
resize gesture can originate from, which doesn't map onto keyboard
interaction at all. A keyboard user who focuses the item gets full
move/resize access regardless of whether a mouse user is restricted to
a specific handle — intentional, matching the Vue/React ports' own
identical reasoning.

### Localizable ARIA strings

The close button's label, `aria-roledescription`, and the keyboard
move/resize instructions are all overridable rather than hardcoded
English literals, via the same `IGridAriaLabels` interface Vue and
React use — see [ARIA labels](/vue/api/interfaces/aria-labels/) (this
package's own API reference for the interface itself is still a
[known gap](/angular/api/)).

## What's not covered (tracked, not silently ignored)

- **No roving-tabindex grid navigation.** Tabbing moves through items in
  DOM order, the same as any other focusable elements on a page.
- **No keyboard equivalent for the drag-from-outside / drag-between-grids
  features** — those are consumer-level example code, not library
  internals.
- **Not independently audited against WCAG success criteria** or run
  through an automated tool (axe, Lighthouse, etc.).
- **Color contrast and the default item styling generally** haven't
  been reviewed.

## Verifying this

`grid-item.component.spec.ts` covers keyboard-accessibility scenarios
at the unit level, including focus attributes present/absent correctly
based on static/edit-mode state, arrow-key movement, and shift+arrow
resize. `e2e/keyboard-accessibility.spec.ts` covers the same ground in
a real browser — a focused item moving/resizing via real key presses,
Tab reachability, and a non-arrow key press correctly doing nothing —
part of this package's own real Playwright e2e suite; see
[Testing philosophy](/angular/guide/project/testing/) for the full
coverage table.
The public methods and fields GridLayoutComponent exposes — the Angular equivalent of Vue's defineExpose or React's imperative handle.

Angular has no separate "imperative handle" type the way React does —
these are simply the `public` methods and fields on the
`GridLayoutComponent` class itself, reached via a template reference
variable:

```ts
import { Component, ViewChild } from '@angular/core';
import { GridLayoutComponent, GridItemComponent } from 'keystone-dashboard-layout-angular';

@Component({
  standalone: true,
  imports: [GridLayoutComponent, GridItemComponent],
  template: `
    <button (click)="grid.compactNow()">Tidy up</button>
    <kdl-grid-layout #grid [layout]="layout" (layoutChange)="layout = $event">
      <!-- ... -->
    </kdl-grid-layout>
  `,
})
export class DashboardComponent {
  @ViewChild('grid') gridRef!: GridLayoutComponent;
  // ...
}
```

A template reference variable (`#grid`, used directly in the template
above via `grid.compactNow()`) works for calling a method from within
the same template. Reach the same instance from your own component
class instead via `@ViewChild('grid')`, as shown.

## Compaction

| Member | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `compactNow` | `(): void` | Re-runs compaction on demand — forces real compaction even when `compactType` is `NONE`, unlike the automatic per-tick compaction. |
| `rearrange` | `(): void` | Alias for `compactNow()`. |

## Items

| Member | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `duplicateItem` | `(id: string \| number): string \| number \| null` | Clones the item, placing the copy directly below the source. Returns the new item's id, or `null` if `id` doesn't match. |
| `scrollToItem` | `(id: string \| number): void` | Scrolls the item into view, if currently rendered. A no-op (not a throw) on a missing id. |
| `focusItem` | `(id: string \| number): void` | Moves keyboard focus to the item, if currently rendered and focusable. |

## Selection (`multiSelect`)

| Member | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `selectedItemIds` | `Set<string \| number>` | The currently-selected item ids. A `Set`, not an array — for O(1) `.has()` lookups. Always empty when `multiSelect` is off. |
| `selectItem` | `(id: string \| number): void` | Selects exactly this item, replacing any existing selection. |
| `deselectItem` | `(id: string \| number): void` | Removes this item from the selection, if present. |
| `toggleItemSelection` | `(id: string \| number): void` | Adds if absent, removes if present. |
| `clearSelection` | `(): void` | Empties the selection entirely. |
| `alignSelected` | `(edge: TAlignEdge): void` | Aligns every selected item to the given edge/center of the anchor (the first-selected item, which never moves). A no-op with fewer than 2 items selected. |
| `distributeSelected` | `(axis: TDistributeAxis): void` | Evenly spaces selected items along the given axis; the two outermost stay fixed. A no-op with fewer than 3 items selected. |

## Undo/redo (`enableUndoRedo`)

| Member | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `undo` | `(): void` | Reverts to the most recently captured pre-gesture snapshot. A no-op when `canUndo` is `false`. |
| `redo` | `(): void` | Reapplies the most recently undone state. A no-op when `canRedo` is `false`. |
| `canUndo` | `boolean` | Whether `undo()` currently has a snapshot to revert to. |
| `canRedo` | `boolean` | Whether `redo()` currently has a snapshot to reapply. |

:::note[canUndo/canRedo are plain fields, not signals or observables]
Reading `gridRef.canUndo` from your own component class won't
automatically re-render your own template when it changes — Angular's
change detection picks it up on the *grid's own* next check (already
triggered internally via `markForCheck()` whenever these change), but
if you're mirroring the value into your own component's state for a
disabled-button binding, you'll need your own mechanism to know when
to re-read it, the same class of consideration React's snapshot-style
`canUndo`/`canRedo` on its own imperative handle requires.
:::

## Export

| Member | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `exportLayoutAsSvg` | `(options?: IExportLayoutAsSvgOptions): string` | Renders the current layout as a standalone SVG string, pre-filled with this grid's own `colNum`/`rowHeight`/`margin`/measured width. |

| Member | Type | Description |

| `containerWidth` | `number` | The measured container pixel width. |

How Keystone Dashboard Layout for Angular compares to GridStack.js, Katoid Angular Grid Layout, and angular-gridster2 — verified directly against each project's own source, docs, and issue tracker.

## Scope

This compares projects in the same category as this library —
**draggable/resizable dashboard layout engines** (position arbitrary
widgets on a grid, drag/resize them, responsive breakpoints) — not data
tables/grids, which solve a different problem. For commercial
layout-engine peers, see
[Comparison: commercial](/angular/guide/project/comparison-commercial/)
instead.

Projects compared: **`gridstack.js`** (framework-agnostic, ships
official Angular/React/Vue wrappers), **Katoid Angular Grid Layout**
(`@katoid/angular-grid-layout`, an Angular-native port of
`react-grid-layout`'s own algorithm), **`angular-gridster2`** (the
long-running, most widely-adopted Angular-specific dashboard grid),
and **Ignite UI Tile Manager** (Infragistics' own tile-layout web
component — new, and worth a methodology note of its own: see below).

**Every claim below was independently verified this session** — READMEs
and API docs read directly, GitHub issues opened and their actual
status/labels checked, config-option source files read line by line —
not taken from a single secondary report. Specific citations are
called out inline. Where a feature genuinely couldn't be confirmed
either way, this page still says so plainly: **"Not established"**
means direct research didn't turn up evidence either way, not proof
the feature is absent.

A distinct note on **Ignite UI Tile Manager**: it's a genuinely
different kind of entry on this page. Infragistics is a commercial
component vendor, and Tile Manager itself is brand new (introduced in
Ignite UI for Angular 19.2, April 2025) — but as of December 2025,
Infragistics made Ignite UI open source (MIT license) across Angular,
Blazor, React, and Web Components, Tile Manager included. It's listed
here rather than in [Comparison: commercial](/angular/guide/project/comparison-commercial/)
because it's genuinely free and MIT-licensed today, not because it
lacks a commercial pedigree — worth knowing given how recent that
licensing change is, and that it doesn't have the multi-year
community track record the other three options on this page do.

## Where this project genuinely leads

Cross-referencing the table above, the features with **no equivalent
confirmed in any of the four alternatives**: cross-grid drag-and-drop
between independent grid instances (`gridstack.js` only offers nested
sub-grids, a different capability; the other three don't document this
at all), magnetic snap-to-grid, visual alignment guides, the
blocked-move feedback event, named layout presets, grid-to-SVG
export, localizable ARIA strings as a dedicated prop surface,
live-resyncing per-item `autoHeight`, undo/redo, and a built-in
click-to-select multi-selection UI (Katoid's own group-transform
mechanics require the consumer to manage selection state externally).
None of these are exotic — they're real-world friction points
(hand-rolled persistence, a hand-wired collision-shake animation,
English-only screen reader text) this library's own roadmap process
exists specifically to find and close one at a time.

Three gaps worth naming with real specificity, not just generic
"ahead": **keyboard accessibility** — `gridstack.js` maintainers
explicitly closed a 2017 accessibility request as `wontfix`, and
neither Katoid, `angular-gridster2`, nor Tile Manager's own
documentation establishes keyboard move/resize at all — where this
library treats it as a baseline, always-available interaction.
**Resize granularity** — Katoid's own README lists full 8-edge resize
as an open TODO item, currently supporting only the bottom-right
corner. And **maximize/restore**, addressed below.

## Where this project is genuinely behind, or simply unconfirmed

- **Maximize/restore an item to fill the surface.** Tile Manager's own
  docs describe this as base, built-in behavior. This library doesn't
  have it yet — the same real, confirmed gap noted against DevExpress
  Dashboard on [Comparison: commercial](/angular/guide/project/comparison-commercial/),
  now also true against a genuinely free, open-source option. Tracked
  on the [Roadmap](/angular/guide/project/roadmap/).
- **RTL support, specifically against `angular-gridster2`.** Its own
  `dirType` config option and a real history of dedicated RTL bug
  fixes confirm this is a mature, exercised feature there — this
  library's own RTL support is real too (see
  [Features](/angular/features/)), but the two haven't been compared
  side by side for parity.
- **Swap-on-drag**, present in both `gridstack.js` (default top-gravity
  mode) and `angular-gridster2` (`swapWhileDragging`). This library only
  pushes items aside via compaction — an item landing on another never
  swaps with it. Not currently tracked on this library's own
  [Roadmap](/angular/guide/project/roadmap/).
- **Ecosystem size and battle-testing.** `angular-gridster2` in
  particular has a multi-year history, hundreds of thousands of weekly
  downloads, and roughly 1,300 GitHub stars — meaningfully more
  production usage than this library can currently claim.
- **Touch device support, confirmed and documented.** Both Katoid and
  `gridstack.js` document touch support directly in their own READMEs.
  This library's drag/resize engine is built on Pointer Events (which
  spec-level covers touch), but no dedicated touch-input e2e spec
  exists yet to confirm it end to end — see
  [Testing philosophy](/angular/guide/project/testing/).
- **Sub-grids / nesting.** `gridstack.js` supports grids-within-grids
  as first-class nested structures (`subGridOpts`, `makeSubGrid()`).
  This library's cross-grid feature is sibling-to-sibling dragging
  between independent grid instances — a different capability, not a
  nesting system.
- **A framework-agnostic core, specifically.** `gridstack.js` ships one
  core engine reused across its Angular/React/Vue wrappers, the same
  architecture this library uses
  (`keystone-dashboard-layout-core` shared across the Vue/React/
  Angular ports). Katoid and `angular-gridster2` are both
  Angular-only throughout, with no separate framework-agnostic core to
  point to.

## Bottom line

Against the three Angular-specific options, this project has a
meaningfully larger feature set on the layout-mechanics and editor-UX
side (cross-grid drag, snap/alignment guides, undo/redo, named
presets, SVG export, a genuine built-in multi-select UI), backed by
direct verification rather than assumption — including two real,
maintainer-acknowledged gaps in Katoid specifically (resize
granularity, static items) found by reading its own README's TODO
list. `angular-gridster2` brings meaningfully more production maturity
and ecosystem size to the table, plus two genuine features this
project doesn't have (swap-on-drag, and RTL support that's been
battle-tested through several real bug fixes). Ignite UI Tile Manager
is the newest and least battle-tested of the four, but already has a
real feature this project lacks — maximize/restore — and is worth
watching given Infragistics' own resources behind it, even though its
Angular support today is a raw web component rather than a first-class
Angular API. `gridstack.js` remains the closest architectural peer (a
shared, framework-agnostic core plus thin per-framework wrappers, now
including React and Vue too) — with a comparably broad but
differently-shaped feature set, and a real, citable accessibility gap
(a 2017 keyboard-support request closed `wontfix`) this library
specifically doesn't share.
How GridLayoutComponent and GridItemComponent talk to each other, and how the codebase is organized.

The map worth knowing before digging deeper into how this port is
built — `GridLayoutComponent` and `GridItemComponent` carry almost the
entire implementation, and their relationship isn't obvious from
reading either file in isolation. This package is a genuine Angular
implementation, not a thin wrapper generated from the Vue source — the
underlying grid math is shared via `keystone-dashboard-layout-core`,
but the component layer itself is idiomatic Angular throughout
(standalone components, `OnPush` change detection, RxJS).

## Two entry points

The main package entry (`GridLayoutComponent`, `GridItemComponent`, and
everything that needs a live component instance or DOM) is one thing; a
separate `keystone-dashboard-layout-core` package is the pure
grid-layout math those components are built on — collision detection,
compaction, movement, alignment guides, breakpoint resolution,
serialization, and validation — with zero Angular dependency for the
vast majority of it. This is the same `core` package the Vue and React
ports use underneath, not a separate copy.

## How GridLayoutComponent and GridItemComponent talk to each other

A consumer renders `GridItemComponent`s themselves, projected via
`<ng-content>` — `GridLayoutComponent` doesn't create your items for
you.

Vue's own port uses a `$parent`-lookup-plus-eventBus contract for this
relationship; React's own uses Context. This package uses **Angular's
own dependency injection**, via a dedicated `GridEventBusService`:

```ts
@Component({
  providers: [GridEventBusService],
  // ...
})
export class GridLayoutComponent { /* ... */ }
```

Provided at the `GridLayoutComponent` level (not `providedIn: 'root'`)
— Angular's DI naturally scopes it to that component's own subtree, one
independent instance per `GridLayout`, matching Vue's own per-instance
eventBus rather than a single app-wide singleton. Two directions of
traffic:

- **Top-down**: `BehaviorSubject`s for grid-wide state a late-subscribing
  `GridItemComponent` still needs immediately (`containerWidth$`,
  `colNum$`, `gridDefaults$`, and so on) — the RxJS analog of Vue's own
  `thisLayout?.propName` reads.
- **Bottom-up**: plain `Subject`s for one-shot gesture events
  (`itemDrag$`, `itemResize$`, `itemClicked$`) — `GridItemComponent`
  reports a drag/resize/click tick; `GridLayoutComponent` subscribes and
  resolves collisions/compaction in response.

RxJS was the deliberate choice here over porting `core`'s own
mitt-style event emitter directly — `BehaviorSubject`/`Subject` are the
idiomatic Angular primitives for exactly this "current value plus a
stream of one-shot events" shape.

## A duplicated cross-grid registry — for a real, confirmed reason

`allowCrossGridDrag` needs separate `GridLayoutComponent` instances —
frequently with no Angular ancestor/descendant injector relationship to
each other at all — to find one another. Vue and React both solve this
with a plain, module-level registry living in
`keystone-dashboard-layout-core` itself. This package keeps its own
**local copy** of that same registry (`cross-grid-registry.ts`) instead
of importing `core`'s — not a stylistic choice or an oversight, but a
confirmed, long-standing `ng-packagr` limitation: `ng-packagr`'s own
Ivy partial compilation can't reliably resolve a *linked* workspace
dependency's secondary `exports` subpaths (the same subpath mechanism
React's own `useCrossGridDrag.ts` relies on to resolve cleanly). The
logic itself is still a direct port — Angular's own `handleCrossGridDragEnd`
was written by reading React's own `useCrossGridDrag.ts` directly, since
that file is already a clean, framework-agnostic reference with nothing
React-specific left in it beyond its own hook wrapper.

## Testing implications

`GridLayoutComponent` and `GridItemComponent` are tested together,
mounting a real `GridLayoutComponent` with real `GridItemComponent`
children projected into it — the only way to exercise the
`GridEventBusService` contract the way production actually uses it. See
[Testing philosophy](/angular/guide/project/testing/) for the fuller
picture.

How Keystone Dashboard Layout for Angular compares to Kendo UI TileLayout, Syncfusion Dashboard Layout, DevExpress Dashboard, Sencha Ext JS Dashboard, and Vaadin Dashboard — verified directly against each vendor's own documentation.

## Scope, and why this is separate from Comparison: alternatives

[Comparison: alternatives](/angular/guide/project/comparison-alternatives/)
scopes itself to open-source peers. This page covers five commercial
products instead. Kendo's actual component is called **TileLayout**
(available for jQuery, **Angular**, React, and Blazor) — this package
has a real, direct competitor here. **Syncfusion** ships a dedicated
**Angular Dashboard Layout** component, the closest of the five to a
general-purpose drop-in competitor. **DevExpress Dashboard** is a full
BI platform, not a standalone layout component — this page compares
against just its layout-authoring piece, since that's the only part in
the same category as this library. **Sencha Ext JS Dashboard**
(`Ext.dashboard.Dashboard`, accessible from Angular via the commercial
`@sencha/ext-angular` wrapper) is a real, long-standing dashboard
component built on an architecture unlike any of the other four — see
below. **Vaadin Dashboard** is a genuinely modern, actively-engineered
component with a real accessibility story — confirmed as a paid
Pro-tier component, not part of Vaadin's free Apache-2.0 core, and
worth a licensing/Angular-fit note of its own too.

Every claim below was independently verified against each vendor's own
current documentation, README, and API reference — not taken from a
single secondary report. The most load-bearing claims are quoted
directly. **"Not established"** still means the reviewed documentation
didn't confirm baseline-equivalent behavior, not proof the feature is
absent.

A note on **Vaadin Dashboard**'s fit here specifically: Vaadin's own
first-class framework integrations are Java (Flow) and React (Hilla) —
there is no dedicated Angular package. The underlying `vaadin-dashboard`
is a standard web component, so it's technically usable from Angular
via `CUSTOM_ELEMENTS_SCHEMA`, the same pattern Ignite UI Tile Manager
uses (see [Comparison: alternatives](/angular/guide/project/comparison-alternatives/))
— but Vaadin's own docs, examples, and typed bindings don't cover
Angular specifically, unlike the other four entries on this page.

## Architecture: four different models, not one

Kendo TileLayout and DevExpress Dashboard both build on structures
where resizing means dragging a **separator line** between adjacent
items, not independent per-item handles — Kendo's own docs describe
its layout as CSS Grid-based with `colSpan`/`rowSpan`, while DevExpress
Dashboard uses a recursive binary split-pane tree of layout groups.
**Ext JS Dashboard** is a third variant on the same theme: a
**column-stack layout**, confirmed directly in its own API docs —
`Ext.layout.container.Dashboard` "extends `Ext.layout.container.Column`
and adds splitters between adjacent columns allowing the user to
resize them." Items ("Parts") stack vertically within a column and
resize **only vertically**, dragged from the bottom edge — column
*width* is what the splitters adjust, not individual item width. This
library uses **freeform, independent `x`/`y`/`w`/`h` grid
coordinates** instead — the same general shape Syncfusion's own
Dashboard Layout and Vaadin Dashboard both use, though the two aren't
identical to each other or to this library: Syncfusion uses
grid-structured panels with upward-floating auto-arrangement,
functionally similar to this library's own vertical compaction, while
Vaadin's own docs describe widgets "placed in columns and rows
automatically, in the order supplied" with the **column count itself
adjusting responsively** to the dashboard's width — closer to a
responsive masonry/auto-flow model than fixed freeform coordinates.
None of these four approaches is strictly better — a constrained model
(Kendo, DevExpress, Ext JS) structurally guarantees no overlaps at the
cost of items never being fully independent of their neighbors;
freeform or auto-flow coordinates (this library, Syncfusion, Vaadin)
give more independent placement, at the cost of needing an explicit
collision/compaction system.

## Honest summary

Against **Kendo TileLayout**: a genuine, direct competitor for Angular
consumers specifically — this library is ahead on nearly every drag/
resize/layout-mechanics dimension: full 8-edge independent resize vs.
a single resize handler plus CSS Grid auto-flow, freeform positioning
vs. reorder-within-auto-flow, cross-grid drag, outside drop, snap/
alignment guides, undo/redo, and multi-select group operations.
Kendo's genuine advantages: being one component in a large commercial
suite with paid support, and per-item lock-against-rearrangement
documented directly (matching this library's own `isStatic`). One
nuance worth being direct about: Kendo's own documentation is
internally inconsistent on whether TileLayout has keyboard support at
all — its dedicated docs and API say yes, its shared package-overview
page says no.

Against **Syncfusion Dashboard Layout**: architecturally one of the
closer matches of the five, since it uses a freeform-ish grid model
with automatic compaction rather than separator-drag resizing — and
the one commercial product here with a real, unambiguously documented
accessibility gap this library specifically closes: Syncfusion's own
accessibility documentation states, verbatim, that keyboard support
does not apply to Dashboard Layout at all, where this library treats
keyboard move/resize as a first-class, always-available interaction
path (see [Accessibility scope](/angular/guide/project/accessibility/)).
Beyond that, this library is ahead on cross-grid drag, outside drop,
snap/alignment guides, undo/redo, multi-select, and SVG export — none
of which Syncfusion's own reviewed documentation establishes.
Syncfusion's genuine advantages: commercial support, built-in themes,
and a responsive single-column auto-stacking behavior with a
configurable media-query breakpoint that's more turnkey than authoring
per-breakpoint layouts by hand.

Against **DevExpress Dashboard**: not a real competitor for most
consumers — it's a BI-authoring product where drag/resize layout is
one supporting piece of a much larger data-analytics platform, not a
drop-in general-purpose layout primitive. The one genuine, real,
API-confirmed gap even at the pure layout-mechanics level is
**maximize/restore** (`MaximizeDashboardItem`/`RestoreDashboardItem`)
— tracked on the [Roadmap](/angular/guide/project/roadmap/), not yet
designed. Its own "Multiselection" feature is worth being precise
about too: it's a BI cross-filtering interaction (select data points
across items to filter a dashboard), a genuinely different concept
from this library's own layout-editing multi-select group move/resize
— not a feature this library is behind on, just a different one
wearing a similar name.

Against **Sencha Ext JS Dashboard**: a real, long-standing component
(the API class dates back years, still documented in current Ext JS
releases), but built on a meaningfully more constrained architecture —
column-stack with inter-column splitters, vertical-only per-item
resize, and drag-to-a-different-column/row rather than free
positioning. This library is ahead on essentially every layout-
mechanics dimension: full 8-edge resize vs. vertical-only, freeform
positioning vs. column-slot placement, cross-grid drag, snap/alignment
guides, undo/redo, and multi-select. Ext JS Dashboard's own genuine
strength, confirmed directly: **per-item lock against drag/resize**
with a real, documented example (specific "parts" configured as
neither draggable nor resizable while others stay interactive) — the
same shape as this library's own `isStatic`, independently confirmed
rather than assumed. Angular access is real but requires the
commercial `@sencha/ext-angular` layer on top of an Ext JS Enterprise
license — a meaningfully bigger commitment than installing an npm
package.

Against **Vaadin Dashboard**: the most interesting comparison on this
page, and the one commercial product here with a genuinely comparable
keyboard-accessibility story — Vaadin's own engineering writeup
confirms dedicated keyboard-based equivalents for moving and resizing
widgets, not just pointer gestures, with a stated WCAG 2.1 AA target.
This library is still ahead on cross-grid drag, outside drop, snap/
alignment guides, named presets, undo/redo, SVG export, and multi-select
— none of which Vaadin's own reviewed documentation establishes — but
Vaadin's responsive auto-flow column model (confirmed: column count
adjusts automatically to the dashboard's width) is a genuinely
different, well-engineered take on responsiveness worth knowing about
even where it isn't a feature gap either way. The real practical
caveat: Vaadin has no dedicated Angular integration at all — a
consumer would be reaching for a raw web component with none of the
Angular-specific documentation, typing, or examples the other four
entries on this page provide.

## What's not worth chasing from any of the five

- **Kendo's CSS Grid-based, single-handle resize model** — adopting
  this would be a regression, not a gap to close.
- **DevExpress's recursive split-pane structure itself**, or **Ext JS
  Dashboard's column-stack-with-splitters model** — rebuilding around
  either architecture would abandon the freeform positioning model
  that's core to what this library is.
- **DevExpress's BI/data-analytics layer entirely** — a different
  product category by design.
- **DevExpress's "Multiselection" concept as named** — a data-filtering
  feature, not a layout one; this library's own multi-select already
  covers the layout-editing use case that name might suggest.
- **Syncfusion's "keyboard support not applicable" stance** — this
  library treats keyboard accessibility as a baseline requirement, not
  an optional extra to skip.
An honest checklist of what's actually verified, what's a known gap, and what's blocking real-world use — not a marketing claim.

## Unit & component tests — Jest + jest-preset-angular

Pure-function tests for the grid math live in
`keystone-dashboard-layout-core` (shared with the Vue and React
ports). This package's own tests cover `GridLayoutComponent`,
`GridItemComponent`, `GridItemDragHandleComponent`,
`GridItemCloseButtonComponent`, and the two services
(`GridLayoutStorageService`, `GridLayoutPresetsService`), run against
`jsdom`.

```sh
pnpm test              # single run
pnpm test:coverage     # single run with coverage
pnpm test:mutation     # mutation tests (Stryker)
```

Jest + `jest-preset-angular` was chosen over Karma for unit/component
testing — mature, widely used for Angular testing, and (unlike the
Vitest-based paths this project tried first) actually available for
this package's Angular `^19.0.0` target: Angular's own first-party
Vitest builder only exists from v20 (experimental) / v21 (stable), and
the third-party Vite/Angular integration route hit a genuinely
unresolved upstream ecosystem bug. Karma (`angular.json`'s own
project-scoped `test` architect target, plus `karma.conf.js`) is kept
in the repository, predating the real e2e layer below, but isn't used
for unit/component tests at all.

### A real, confirmed Stryker/Jest interaction worth knowing about

`@stryker-mutator/jest-runner`'s own sandbox resolved
`jest-preset-angular`'s implicit `testEnvironment` default differently
than plain `jest` does — surfacing as `ReferenceError: document is not
defined` plus an Angular DI circular-dependency cascade, not a subtle
timing issue. Fixed with an explicit `testEnvironment: 'jsdom'` in
`jest.config.ts`. Worth knowing if a future change to the test config
resurfaces something similar.

### Component testing approach

`GridLayoutComponent` and `GridItemComponent` are tested together,
rendering a real `GridLayoutComponent` with real `GridItemComponent`
children projected into it — the same shape actual usage takes, so the
`GridEventBusService` contract (see
[Architecture](/angular/guide/project/architecture/)) behaves exactly
as it does in production, rather than relying on a hand-rolled fake
service.

A few things need handling, since `jsdom` can't provide them natively:

- **`ResizeObserver`** — `jsdom` doesn't implement it at all.
  Replaced with a stub for most tests.
- **The native drag/resize engine's own pointer handling** — shared
  with the Vue and React ports via `keystone-dashboard-layout-core`;
  tests invoke the component's actual drag/resize handling logic
  directly rather than simulating a full, real pointer gesture through
  `jsdom`.

### Notes on interaction tests

Drag and resize tests drive real pointer input (mouse down → move in
steps → up) rather than clicking a locator, since the native engine
needs a real sequence of pointer events to recognize a drag/resize
gesture — a single click won't trigger it. Same rationale, and the same
underlying native engine (`keystone-dashboard-layout-core`), as the
Vue and React ports' own e2e tests. A few assertions specifically use a
`stableBoundingBox()` helper (`e2e/helpers.ts`) rather than a single
`boundingBox()` read — a CSS transition still settling at the exact
moment of measurement was a real, confirmed source of flakiness in
early runs, not a hypothetical one.

The interface backing localizable ARIA strings, plus the built-in English defaults exported alongside it.
The interface behind the compactor prop, its context object, and the five built-in strategies exported alongside it.

```ts
interface ICompactor {
  readonly type: string;
  compact(layout: TLayout, cols: number, context: ICompactorContext): TLayout;
}
```

| Member | Description |
|---|---|
| `type` | A short, descriptive name for this strategy — informational only (e.g. for logging); never read by `GridLayout` itself. |
| `compact(layout, cols, context)` | Compacts a layout, **returning a new array** — must not mutate the input `layout` or any of its items in place. |

| Field | Description |
|---|---|
| `compactType` | Which built-in strategy currently applies — informational, read from `GridLayout`'s own `compactType` prop at the moment compaction runs. A custom compactor decides for itself whether/how to use this; nothing enforces it. |
| `minPositions` | Present only during a `restoreOnDrag`-gated compaction (drag end) — the pre-drag position each item shouldn't rise/shift any tighter than. Absent for every other trigger (resize end, add/remove, mount, breakpoint change, `compactNow()`/`rearrange()`), and for the two `*_OVERLAP` types. |

## The five built-in strategies

Exported individually, as a starting point for a custom compactor to
delegate back to for part of a layout (e.g. compact everything except
one pinned row) rather than reimplementing standard compaction from
scratch. `ICompactor` itself and all five strategies below live in
`keystone-dashboard-layout-core`, not this package's own barrel:

```ts
import {
  verticalCompactor,
  horizontalCompactor,
  noCompactor,
  verticalOverlapCompactor,
  horizontalOverlapCompactor,
  getCompactor,
} from 'keystone-dashboard-layout-core';
```

| Export | Backs |
|---|---|
| `verticalCompactor` | `ECompactType.VERTICAL` (the default) |
| `horizontalCompactor` | `ECompactType.HORIZONTAL` |
| `noCompactor` | `ECompactType.NONE` |
| `verticalOverlapCompactor` | `ECompactType.VERTICAL_OVERLAP` |
| `horizontalOverlapCompactor` | `ECompactType.HORIZONTAL_OVERLAP` |
| `getCompactor(compactType)` | Looks up the built-in `ICompactor` matching a given `ECompactType` — the same mapping `GridLayout` itself uses internally when the `compactor` prop isn't set. |

See [Pluggable compaction](/react/examples/pluggable-compaction/) for a
full working custom compactor, and [ECompactType](/react/api/enums/compact-type/)
for what each built-in strategy actually does.
The typed payloads for GridLayout's cross-grid and outside-drop callbacks.
The ref-based API GridLayout exposes — the React equivalent of Vue's defineExpose template-ref methods.

Attach a `ref` to `GridLayout` to reach these — the React equivalent of
Vue's own `defineExpose`'d template-ref methods, via `forwardRef`/
`useImperativeHandle` instead.

```tsx
import { useRef } from 'react';
import { GridLayout, type IGridLayoutHandle } from 'keystone-dashboard-layout-react';

function Dashboard() {
  const gridRef = useRef<IGridLayoutHandle>(null);

  return (
    <>
      <button onClick={() => gridRef.current?.compactNow()}>Tidy up</button>
      <GridLayout ref={gridRef} layout={layout} onLayoutChange={setLayout}>
        {/* ... */}
      </GridLayout>
    </>
  );
}
```

## Compaction

| Member | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `compactNow` | `() => void` | Re-runs compaction on demand — forces real compaction even when `compactType` is `NONE`, unlike the automatic per-tick compaction. |
| `rearrange` | `() => void` | Alias for `compactNow()`. |

## Items

| Member | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `duplicateItem` | `(id: string \| number) => string \| number \| null` | Clones the item, placing the copy directly below the source. Returns the new item's id, or `null` if `id` doesn't match. |
| `scrollToItem` | `(id: string \| number) => Promise<void>` | Scrolls the item into view, if currently rendered. A no-op (not a throw) on a missing id. |
| `focusItem` | `(id: string \| number) => Promise<void>` | Moves keyboard focus to the item, if currently rendered and focusable. |

## Selection (`multiSelect`)

| Member | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `selectedItems` | `(string \| number)[]` | The currently-selected item ids, in selection order. |
| `selectItem` | `(id: string \| number) => void` | Adds an item to the selection. A no-op when `multiSelect` is off. |
| `deselectItem` | `(id: string \| number) => void` | Removes an item from the selection, if present. |
| `toggleItemSelection` | `(id: string \| number) => void` | Adds if absent, removes if present. |
| `clearSelection` | `() => void` | Empties the selection entirely. |
| `alignSelected` | `(edge: TAlignEdge) => void` | Aligns every selected item to the given edge/center of the anchor (the first-selected item, which never moves). A no-op with fewer than 2 items selected. |
| `distributeSelected` | `(axis: TDistributeAxis) => void` | Evenly spaces selected items along the given axis; the two outermost stay fixed. A no-op with fewer than 3 items selected. |

## Undo/redo (`enableUndoRedo`)

| Member | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `undo` | `() => void` | Reverts to the layout before the most recent undo-tracked action. A no-op when nothing is available to undo. |
| `redo` | `() => void` | Re-applies the most recently undone action. Redo history clears the moment a fresh action is committed. |
| `canUndo` | `boolean` | Whether `undo()` would currently do anything. |
| `canRedo` | `boolean` | Whether `redo()` would currently do anything. |

## Export

| Member | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `exportLayoutAsSvg` | `(options?: IExportLayoutAsSvgOptions) => string` | Renders the current layout as a standalone SVG string, pre-filled with this grid's own `colNum`/`rowHeight`/`margin`/measured width. |
useLayoutStorage and useLayoutPresets — hooks for saving and loading a layout.
One entry in a GridLayout's layout array — every field a layout item can carry.

One entry in a `GridLayout`'s `layout` array. Unlike Vue's own
`GridItem` (which also accepts most of these directly as component
props), this package's `GridItem` is deliberately minimal — only `i`
is required — so these fields on the matching layout entry are the
*only* way to configure per-item behavior at all, not just an
alternative to component props.

```ts
interface ILayoutItemRequired {
  i: string | number;
  h: number;
  w: number;
  x: number;
  y: number;
}

interface ILayoutItem<TMeta = unknown> extends ILayoutItemRequired {
  // ...optional fields below
}
```

`ILayoutItemRequired` is exported separately too, in case you need to
type just the required fields on their own (a minimal seed object before
optional fields are added, say).

## Required fields

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `i` | `string \| number` | Unique identifier, matched against a `GridItem`'s `i` prop. Must be either a non-empty string or a finite number — never both at once, and never an empty string. String matching against a `GridItem`'s own `i` prop is case-insensitive (`'Widget-1'` matches `'widget-1'`); number matching is exact. |
| `h` | `number` | Height, in grid row units. |
| `w` | `number` | Width, in grid column units. |
| `x` | `number` | Horizontal position, in grid column units. |
| `y` | `number` | Vertical position, in grid row units. |

## Optional fields

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `isDraggable` | `boolean` | Per-item drag override. |
| `isResizable` | `boolean` | Per-item resize override. |
| `isStatic` | `boolean` | Excludes this item from dragging, resizing, and collision cascades. |
| `maxH` / `maxW` / `minH` / `minW` | `number` | Per-item size constraints. |
| `zIndex` | `number \| null` | CSS `z-index` override, winning over the static/dragging/resizing CSS-class defaults. |
| `showCloseButton` | `boolean` | Per-item override; `undefined` defers to the grid-wide default. |
| `autoScroll` | `boolean` | Per-item override for native auto-scroll near a container edge during drag/resize. |
| `preserveAspectRatio` | `boolean` | Per-item override for locking width/height ratio while resizing. |
| `ariaLabels` | `IGridAriaLabels` | Per-item override, merged over the grid-wide `ariaLabels` prop and the built-in English defaults. |
| `dragAllowFrom` / `dragIgnoreFrom` | `string \| null` | CSS selectors restricting where a drag can/can't start. |
| `resizeIgnoreFrom` | `string \| null` | CSS selector for elements that shouldn't start a resize. |
| `dragActivationDistance` | `TDragActivationDistance \| null` | Minimum pointer movement, in pixels, before a pointerdown counts as a drag — one value for every pointer type, or distinct values per mouse/touch/pen. |
| `isBounded` | `boolean \| null` | Per-item override for restricting dragging to within the container. |
| `resizeHandles` | `TResizeHandle[] \| null` | Restricts which of the 8 resize-hint spans render/activate for this item. An empty array is a valid "no handle-driven resize" value, distinct from `isResizable: false`. |
| `isMirrored` | `boolean` | Whether this item participates in the grid's own RTL mirroring. Default `true`. |
| `enableEditMode` | `boolean` | Per-item override for the master interactivity switch. |
| `borderRadiusPx` / `useBorderRadius` | `number` / `boolean` | Per-item border radius override. |
| `showResizeHandles` / `resizeHandleColor` | `boolean` / `string` | Per-item visible resize-handle override. |
| `autoHeight` | `boolean` | Re-runs this item's own size measurement whenever its rendered content changes size. No grid-wide equivalent. |
| `moved` | `boolean` | Set internally by compaction/collision helpers to short-circuit infinite loops — not meant to be set by consumers. |
| `data` | `TMeta` | Optional, consumer-defined payload — never read or written by the library itself. Round-trips through serialize/deserialize like any other field, as long as it's JSON-serializable. |

## `TMeta` — attaching typed data to a layout item

```tsx
interface IWidgetConfig {
  chartType: 'bar' | 'line';
}

const [layout, setLayout] = useState<TLayout<IWidgetConfig>>([
  { h: 2, i: '0', w: 2, x: 0, y: 0, data: { chartType: 'bar' } },
]);
```

Attach whatever payload an item needs directly on the layout item,
instead of maintaining a parallel array keyed by `i` to look it up
separately. Every existing usage of `ILayoutItem`/`TLayout` without a
type argument keeps working unchanged — the default (`unknown`) only
matters if you actually read `.data` and want it typed as something
more specific.

## `TLayoutItem`

Structurally identical to `ILayoutItem`. Both exist in the codebase;
prefer `ILayoutItem` for new code — `TLayoutItem` is kept for backwards
compatibility with existing type annotations.

See [GridItem props](/react/components/grid-item/props/) for the full
table of these fields alongside `GridItem`'s own (much smaller) set of
actual component props.
exportLayoutAsSvg and readOutsideDropPayload — two standalone utility functions.

## `exportLayoutAsSvg`

```ts
function exportLayoutAsSvg(layout: TLayout, options?: IExportLayoutAsSvgOptions): string;
```

```ts
interface IExportLayoutAsSvgOptions {
  colNum?: number;          // default: 12
  rowHeight?: number;       // default: 150
  margin?: [number, number]; // default: [10, 10]
  containerWidth?: number;  // default: 1200 — must be supplied explicitly; see note below
  itemFill?: string;        // default: '#eef2ff'
  itemStroke?: string;      // default: '#c7d2fe'
  labelColor?: string;      // default: '#3730a3'
  backgroundColor?: string | null; // default: null (transparent)
}
```

Renders a `TLayout` as a standalone SVG string, each item drawn as a
labeled rectangle from the layout data alone — not a snapshot of
whatever's actually rendered inside each `GridItem`. Good for a
structural thumbnail of the layout itself, not a substitute for a real
screenshot of custom `children` content. Never throws: an empty layout
produces a valid, empty SVG.

`containerWidth` has to be passed explicitly, unlike `GridLayout`
itself, which measures its own container automatically — there's no
DOM element for this standalone function to measure. Pass the same
width your actual grid renders at for a matching result.

The returned string is a complete `<svg>...</svg>` document — usable
directly, downloaded as a `.svg` file via a `Blob`, or drawn onto a
`<canvas>` first if a raster PNG/JPEG is specifically needed. See
[Export layout as SVG](/react/examples/svg-export/) for a full example.

Not re-exported from this package's own barrel — import it directly
from `keystone-dashboard-layout-core` instead, same as the Vue port:

```ts
import { exportLayoutAsSvg } from 'keystone-dashboard-layout-core';
```

## `readOutsideDropPayload`

```ts
function readOutsideDropPayload<T>(
  dataTransfer: DataTransfer | null | undefined,
  mimeType?: string, // default: 'text/plain'
): T | null;
```

Reads and JSON-parses a native `DataTransfer` payload by MIME type —
every consumer of `allowOutsideDrop`'s `onOutsideDrop` callback
otherwise re-implements the same `dataTransfer.getData(mimeType)`/
`JSON.parse` parsing by hand. Never throws: a missing MIME type or
malformed JSON both return `null`. Performs no runtime shape validation
against `T` — that's the caller's own responsibility, since the payload
is whatever the consumer's own drag source chose to attach.

:::caution[A real gotcha with native drag-and-drop]
`dataTransfer.getData()` only returns real values during the `drop`
event itself — not `dragenter`/`dragover`.
:::

Same as `exportLayoutAsSvg` above, this isn't re-exported from this
package's own barrel either:

```ts
import { readOutsideDropPayload } from 'keystone-dashboard-layout-core';
```

See [outsideDropAccept & readOutsideDropPayload](/react/examples/outside-drop-accept-payload/)
for a full working example.
Every prop GridItem accepts, and where per-item configuration actually lives.

`GridItem` itself is deliberately minimal — only `i` is required.
Everything Vue's own `GridItem` takes as a component prop
(`isDraggable`, `minW`, `zIndex`, and so on) instead lives directly on
the matching entry in `GridLayout`'s own `layout` array (an
`ILayoutItem`, from `keystone-dashboard-layout-core`) — set those
fields on your layout data instead of on this component.

## Component props

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `i` | `string \| number` (required) | — | Matches this item to its entry in the parent `GridLayout`'s `layout` array. Must be either a non-empty string or a finite number — never both at once. String matching is case-insensitive (`'Widget-1'` matches `'widget-1'`); number matching is exact. |
| `header` | `ReactNode` | — | Optional header content, rendered above `children` in a fixed-size row — `children` becomes a scrollable body below it. Omitting this prop entirely renders `children` exactly as before, unaffected. The render-prop equivalent of Vue's own `#header` slot. |
| `children` | `ReactNode` | — | The item's own content — becomes the scrollable body region when `header` is also provided. |
| `renderResizeHandle` | `(edge: TResizeHandle) => ReactNode` | — | Customizes a resize-hint span's own content (an icon, typically) — called once per actually-rendered edge/corner, with that edge's identifier. `undefined` renders each span empty. The render-prop equivalent of Vue's own `#resize-handle` slot. |
| `onItemMoved` | `(payload: { i: string \| number; x: number; y: number }) => void` | — | Fired when this item's own drag gesture ends, with its own final grid-unit `x`/`y` — a direct per-item alternative to reading the same information out of `GridLayout`'s own broader `onLayoutChange`. Matches Vue's own `@item-moved`. Reports this item's own locally-computed, pre-compaction value — `onLayoutChange` remains the source of truth for the fully-compacted result. |
| `onItemResized` | `(payload: { i: string \| number; h: number; w: number; height: number; width: number }) => void` | — | Fired when this item's own resize gesture ends, with its own final grid-unit `h`/`w` *and* pixel `height`/`width` together. Matches Vue's own `@resized`. Same pre-compaction-value timing note as `onItemMoved`. |
| `className` | `string` | — | Applied to the item's own root element, alongside the library's own positioning/interaction classes. |

## Per-item configuration (`ILayoutItem`)

These fields live on the layout item itself — the object in `GridLayout`'s
`layout` array whose `i` matches this `GridItem`'s own `i` prop — not on
`GridItem`. Most mirror a same-named `GridLayout` prop as a per-item
override; `undefined`/`null` defers to that grid-wide default.

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `isDraggable` | `boolean` | Overrides the grid-wide default for this item. |
| `isResizable` | `boolean` | Overrides the grid-wide default for this item. |
| `isStatic` | `boolean` | Excludes this item from dragging, resizing, and collision cascades entirely. |
| `minW` / `maxW` / `minH` / `maxH` | `number` | Size constraints, in grid units. |
| `isBounded` | `boolean \| null` | Overrides the grid-wide `isBounded` default for this item. |
| `zIndex` | `number \| null` | CSS `z-index` override, always winning over the static/dragging/resizing CSS-class-based defaults when set. |
| `showCloseButton` | `boolean` | Overrides the grid-wide default for this item. |
| `autoScroll` | `boolean` | Overrides the grid-wide default for this item. |
| `preserveAspectRatio` | `boolean` | Overrides the grid-wide default for this item. |
| `ariaLabels` | `IGridAriaLabels` | Merged over the grid-wide `ariaLabels` prop (and that, in turn, over the built-in English defaults). |
| `dragAllowFrom` | `string \| null` | CSS selector restricting which descendant elements can start a drag. |
| `dragIgnoreFrom` | `string` | CSS selector for elements that should *not* start a drag. Has no effect when `dragAllowFrom` is also set. Defaults to `` `a, button` `` when left unset, matching Vue. |
| `resizeIgnoreFrom` | `string \| null` | CSS selector for elements that should *not* start a resize. |
| `dragActivationDistance` | `TDragActivationDistance \| null` | Per-pointer-type drag-start threshold for this item. |
| `resizeHandles` | `TResizeHandle[] \| null` | Overrides the grid-wide default for this item. An empty array is a valid "no handle-driven resize for this item" value, distinct from `isResizable: false`. |
| `isMirrored` | `boolean` | Whether this item participates in the grid's own RTL mirroring. Default `true`. |
| `enableEditMode` | `boolean` | Overrides the grid-wide master interactivity switch for this item. |
| `borderRadiusPx` | `number` | Overrides the grid-wide default for this item. |
| `useBorderRadius` | `boolean` | Overrides the grid-wide default for this item. |
| `showResizeHandles` | `boolean` | Overrides the grid-wide default for this item. |
| `resizeHandleColor` | `string` | Overrides the grid-wide default for this item. |
| `autoHeight` | `boolean` | Automatically re-measures this item's own height/width whenever its rendered content changes size, via a `ResizeObserver` — independent of the whole grid being `autoSize`d. |
| `data` | your own type | Optional, consumer-defined payload — never read or written by the library itself. Attach a widget's config or dataset reference directly here instead of maintaining a parallel lookup keyed by `i`. |

See [Layout interface](/react/api/interfaces/layout/) for the full
`ILayoutItem` reference, shared with the Vue package via
`keystone-dashboard-layout-core`.
Every prop GridLayout accepts, including callbacks, with defaults.

Only `layout` is required — everything else has a default.
`GridLayout` is a **fully controlled** component: it never mutates
`layout` in place. Callbacks are ordinary props here (there's no
separate "events" mechanism the way Vue emits — this table includes
them alongside the setter-style props). Most boolean/number props here
have a matching field on [`ILayoutItem`](/react/api/) that can override
it per-item; see each prop's note.

## Core

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `layout` | `TLayout` (required) | — | The layout array — one entry per rendered `GridItem`, matched by `i`. Position, size, and `isDraggable`/`isResizable`/`isStatic`/`minW`/`maxW`/`minH`/`maxH`/`zIndex`/`showCloseButton` all live directly on each entry — there's no separate per-item prop the way Vue's `GridItem` component has, since a `GridItem` here only takes `i` and looks its own data up from this array. |
| `onLayoutChange` | `(layout: TLayout) => void` | — | Called with a brand-new layout array whenever a drag end, resize end, or the compaction that follows either changes it. The input `layout` prop itself is never mutated. |
| `children` | `ReactNode` | — | The `GridItem` elements to render — one per `layout` entry, each needing only a matching `i` prop and a `key`. |
| `className` | `string` | — | Applied to the root element, alongside the library's own `kdl-grid-layout` class. |

## Sizing & columns

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `colNum` | `number` | `12` | Maximum number of columns. |
| `rowHeight` | `number` | `150` | Height of one grid row, in pixels. |
| `margin` | `[number, number]` | `[10, 10]` | `[horizontal, vertical]` spacing between items, in pixels. |
| `maxRows` | `number` | `Infinity` | Maximum number of rows the layout may grow to. |
| `autoSize` | `boolean` | `true` | Deprecated — prefer `heightMode`. Grows/shrinks the container's height to fit the layout's content. Ignored once `heightMode` is set to anything other than `null`. |
| `heightMode` | `'auto' \| 'fixed' \| 'scroll' \| 'fit' \| null` | `null` | How the container's height is determined. `null` defers to `autoSize`. `'auto'`: today's `autoSize: true` behavior. `'fixed'`: no explicit height — today's `autoSize: false`. `'scroll'`: same as `'fixed'`, plus `overflow-y: auto`. `'fit'`: height locked to `100%` of the parent, with the same `overflow-y: auto` as `'scroll'`. |
| `useCssTransforms` | `boolean` | `true` | Positions items via CSS `transform: translate3d(...)` instead of `top`/`left`. |
| `transformScale` | `number` | `1` | Compensates drag/resize pixel math for a scaled ancestor (e.g. a zoomed-out canvas view). |

## Drag & resize defaults

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `isDraggable` | `boolean` | `true` | Default for items that don't set their own `isDraggable`. |
| `isResizable` | `boolean` | `true` | Default for items that don't set their own `isResizable`. |
| `isBounded` | `boolean` | `false` | Restricts dragging to within the container's bounds. A per-item `isBounded` overrides this. |
| `enableEditMode` | `boolean` | `true` | Grid-wide master interactivity switch — `false` disables dragging, resizing, and the close button across the whole grid at once. A per-item `enableEditMode` overrides this. |
| `dragActivationDistance` | — | — | Per-pointer-type drag-start threshold, forwarded to the shared `core` engine. |
| `resizeHandles` | `TResizeHandle[]` | all 8 | Restricts which resize-hint spans render/activate, grid-wide. A per-item `resizeHandles` overrides this (an empty array is a valid "no handle-driven resize" value). |
| `showResizeHandles` | `boolean` | `false` | Renders a visible resize-handle affordance instead of the default invisible hit-zone. A per-item override exists. |
| `resizeHandleColor` | `string` | `'rgb(94 94 94 / 45%)'` | CSS color for the visible resize-handle affordance. A per-item override exists. |
| `preserveAspectRatio` | `boolean` | `false` | Grid-wide default for whether resizing preserves an item's current width/height ratio. A per-item override exists. |
| `autoScroll` | `boolean` | `false` | Grid-wide default for whether native auto-scroll runs near a container edge during drag/resize. A per-item override exists. |

## Collision & compaction

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `preventCollision` | `boolean` | `false` | Blocks a drag/resize that would collide, instead of pushing the other item. |
| `compactType` | `ECompactType` | `ECompactType.VERTICAL` | Selects one of five built-in compaction strategies. Ignored when `compactor` is set. |
| `compactor` | `ICompactor \| null` | `null` | Overrides the built-in compaction algorithm entirely. Purely additive — `compactType` keeps working normally when this isn't set. |
| `horizontalShift` | `boolean` | `false` | Pushes colliding items left/right instead of down, during an active drag. |
| `restoreOnDrag` | `boolean` | `false` | While dragging, keeps other items from compacting past their pre-drag position until the drag ends. |
| `distributeEvenly` | `boolean` | `false` | On a responsive breakpoint change that shrinks `colNum`, spreads an out-of-bounds item to the next available slot instead of clamping it to the right edge. |
| `snapToGrid` | `boolean` | `false` | Magnetically snaps a dragged item's edge to another item's edge — changes where the item lands, unlike `showAlignmentGuides`. |
| `snapThreshold` | `number` | `1` | How close (in grid units) an edge needs to be to snap, when `snapToGrid` is on. `0` disables snapping. |
| `showAlignmentGuides` | `boolean` | `false` | Shows guide lines while dragging/resizing wherever edges line up — visual only. |
| `showSpacingGuides` | `boolean` | `false` | Shows a labeled distance badge between the active item and its nearest neighbor. |
| `onMoveBlockedByCollision` | `(id: string \| number) => void` | — | Called when `preventCollision` actually constrained a drag or resize. |

## Multi-select & undo/redo

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `multiSelect` | `boolean` | `false` | Enables click/Shift-click/Ctrl-click multi-item selection, and group move/resize for the selection. |
| `onSelectionChanged` | `(selectedItems: (string \| number)[]) => void` | — | Called with the full, current selection whenever it changes. Not called on initial mount. |
| `enableUndoRedo` | `boolean` | `false` | Enables `undo()`/`redo()` via the imperative handle. Snapshots are taken at drag start, resize start, `duplicateItem`, `compactNow`, and any externally-driven `layout` length change. |
| `undoHistoryLimit` | `number` | `50` | Maximum number of snapshots kept for `undo()`. |

| `cols` | `IColumns` | `{ xxl: 12, xl: 12, lg: 12, md: 10, sm: 6, xs: 4, xxs: 2 }` | Column count per breakpoint. |

## Styling

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |

| `allowCrossGridDrag` | `boolean` | `false` | Enables dragging an item between two `GridLayout` instances that both have this set, via a real first-fit bin-pack. |
| `disableExternalDrop` | `boolean` | `false` | This grid rejects incoming cross-grid drops. Its own items can still be dragged out. Only relevant when `allowCrossGridDrag` is on. |
| `layoutId` | `string` | auto-generated | This grid's own identifier for the cross-grid registry and event payloads. |
| `onCrossGridItemDropped` | `(payload: ICrossGridItemDropped) => void` | — | Called on the target grid when another grid's item is dropped and accepted. |

| Prop | Type | Description |

Re-exported from the package's main entry point as a real (value)
export, so you can both type `compactType` and compare/construct
against these at runtime.

```ts
enum ECompactType {
  NONE = 'none',
  HORIZONTAL = 'horizontal',
  HORIZONTAL_OVERLAP = 'horizontal-overlap',
  VERTICAL = 'vertical',
  VERTICAL_OVERLAP = 'vertical-overlap',
}
```

| Value | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `NONE` | No compaction at all — items stay exactly where placed, gaps included. Colliding items still get pushed down out of the way; this is distinct from `VERTICAL_OVERLAP` below — turning compaction off has never meant turning collision resolution off too. |
| `HORIZONTAL` | Items compact leftward, floating to the smallest available `x` without colliding with anything already placed. |
| `HORIZONTAL_OVERLAP` | Horizontal compaction, but every non-static item moves straight to `x: 0` unconditionally, ignoring collisions entirely — matching `react-grid-layout`'s own `allowOverlap` semantics applied to compaction specifically. Items may end up visually overlapping as a result. |
| `VERTICAL` (default) | Items compact upward, floating to the smallest available `y` without colliding with anything already placed. |
| `VERTICAL_OVERLAP` | Vertical compaction, but every non-static item moves straight to `y: 0` unconditionally, ignoring collisions. Same overlap semantics as `HORIZONTAL_OVERLAP`, applied to the vertical axis. |

Replaces an older, separate `verticalCompact: boolean` prop — a single
enum-valued prop is easier to extend (the two `*_OVERLAP` members add a
capability the boolean couldn't express at all) and easier to reason
about than a growing pile of independent booleans.

See [Pluggable compaction](/vue/api/interfaces/compactor/) for the
`compactor` prop that lets you replace the algorithm entirely instead
of picking one of these five, and [Pluggable compaction (compactType &
compactor)](/vue/examples/pluggable-compaction/) for a live demo
switching between all five plus a custom compactor.

How GridLayout and GridItem talk to each other, and how the codebase is organized.

The map worth knowing before digging deeper into how this port is
built — `GridLayout` and `GridItem` carry almost the entire
implementation, and their relationship isn't obvious from reading either
file in isolation. This package is a genuine React implementation, not
a thin wrapper generated from the Vue source — the underlying grid math
is shared via `keystone-dashboard-layout-core`, but the component
layer itself is idiomatic React throughout.

## Two entry points

The main package entry (`GridLayout`, `GridItem`, and everything that
needs a live component instance or DOM) is one thing; a separate
`keystone-dashboard-layout-core` package is the pure grid-layout math
those components are built on — collision detection, compaction,
movement, alignment guides, breakpoint resolution, serialization, and
validation — with zero React dependency and no live DOM required for
the vast majority of it. This is the same `core` package the Vue port
uses underneath, not a separate copy.

## A fully controlled component

`GridLayout` never mutates its `layout` prop in place. Every internal
change (a drag tick, a resize tick, the compaction that follows either)
is mirrored into local state *and* reported via `onLayoutChange` —
matching `react-grid-layout`'s own established contract for this class
of component, since that's the idiomatic React pattern here rather than
Vue's `v-model:layout` two-way binding. Compaction re-runs on every
single drag/resize tick, not only at the gesture's end — this is what
produces the "other items shuffle out of the way live, while you're
still dragging" feedback, not just a final snap-into-place at drop.

## How GridLayout and GridItem talk to each other

A consumer renders `GridItem`s themselves, as `GridLayout`'s `children`
— `GridLayout` doesn't create your items for you.

Vue's own port uses a `$parent`-lookup-plus-eventBus contract for this
relationship (see that port's own [Architecture](/vue/guide/project/architecture/)
page). This package expresses the identical relationship using React's
own `createContext`/`useContext` instead, since that's the idiomatic
mechanism for "many descendants read shared ancestor state and report
back up" in React:

- **Top-down**: a single `GridContext` value carries the live working
  layout, every relevant grid-wide setting (`colNum`, `margin`,
  `isDraggable`, `resizeHandles`, resolved ARIA labels, and so on), and
  the callbacks a `GridItem` calls to report its own drag/resize/click
  activity.
- **Bottom-up**: `GridItem` calls `onItemDrag`/`onItemResize`/
  `onItemClick` (all part of the same context value) to report gesture
  ticks — `GridLayout`'s own handlers resolve collisions/bounds and
  update the working layout in response.

A `GridItem` rendered outside a `GridLayout` throws a clear error
(`GridItem must be rendered inside a GridLayout.`) rather than silently
reading `undefined` fields — the same "reachable only in this
configuration" invariant Vue's own `$parent` lookup already depends on,
made explicit here instead of failing confusingly later.

## Render-props instead of slots

Vue's own `GridItem`/`GridLayout` expose scoped slots (`#header`,
`#resize-handle`, `#placeholder`) for customizing rendered content. This
package uses React's own idiomatic equivalent — render props
(`header`, `renderResizeHandle`, `renderPlaceholder`) — rather than
introducing a slot-like abstraction React doesn't otherwise have. See
[GridLayout props](/react/components/grid-layout/props/) and
[GridItem props](/react/components/grid-item/props/) for the full list.

## Native drag/resize engine

Both drag and resize wire up a native, Pointer Events-based engine —
the same one Vue's port uses, from `keystone-dashboard-layout-core`
(`createNativeDraggable`/`createNativeResizable`). No third-party
drag/resize library at all, and no separate React-specific copy of this
engine — it's genuinely framework-agnostic (built on the plain Pointer
Events API), so both ports share one implementation. Each gesture is
guarded to one pointer at a time per element, so a second concurrent
pointer (two fingers, an accidental palm touch mid-drag) can't silently
hijack tracking.

## Cross-grid drag/drop

`allowCrossGridDrag` needs separate `GridLayout` instances — frequently
with no React ancestor/descendant relationship to each other at all —
to find one another. Same answer as Vue's port: a plain, module-level
registry (not React state, not Context), where every participating grid
registers itself on mount and deregisters on unmount. See
[Drag, drop from grid to grid](/react/examples/cross-grid-drag-drop/).

## Testing implications

`GridLayout` and `GridItem` are tested together, rendering a real
`GridLayout` with real `GridItem` children — the only way to exercise
the Context contract the way production actually uses it. See
[Testing philosophy](/react/guide/project/testing/) for the fuller
picture.
