## Scope

This compares projects in the same category as this library —
**draggable/resizable dashboard layout engines** (position arbitrary
widgets on a grid, drag/resize them, responsive breakpoints) — not data
tables/grids, which solve a different problem. For commercial
layout-engine peers, see
[Comparison: commercial](/react/guide/project/comparison-commercial/)
instead.

Projects compared: **`react-grid-layout`** (the long-established
incumbent in this exact category, recently rewritten with a hooks-based
v2) and **`gridstack.js`** (framework-agnostic, ships an official React
wrapper).

## A different landscape than Vue's own comparison

Unlike the Vue port's own [Comparison: alternatives](/vue/guide/project/comparison-alternatives/)
page — where the most-starred option still has no official Vue 3
release, and the field is a handful of differently-maintained community
forks — React's own landscape has a genuine, well-established incumbent:
`react-grid-layout` is mature, widely adopted, and actively maintained,
recently rewritten with a hooks-based v2. This is the honest starting
point for a React-specific comparison: this package is the newer
entrant here, not filling an obvious gap the way the Vue port arguably
is.

## Feature comparison

The facts below for `react-grid-layout` v2 and `gridstack.js` are the
same ones already verified for the Vue port's own comparison page — the
features themselves are properties of those two projects, not of which
framework is being compared against.

| Feature | This project | `react-grid-layout` v2 | `gridstack.js` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cross-grid drag/drop (independent instances) | Yes | No | Via nested sub-grids — a different mechanism |
| Drag-and-drop from outside the component | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Magnetic snap-to-grid | Yes | No | No |
| Visual alignment guides | Yes | No | No |
| Blocked-move feedback event | Yes | No | No |
| Named layout presets | Yes | No | No |
| First-party persistence helper | Yes | No | Yes, built into the core engine |
| Grid-to-SVG export | Yes | No | No |
| Localizable UI/ARIA strings | Yes | No | No |
| Per-item live-resyncing autoHeight | Yes | No | Partial — content-driven initial sizing only |
| Keyboard-only move/resize | Yes | No | No |
| Multi-select + group move/resize | Yes | Not confirmed | Not confirmed |
| Pluggable compaction algorithm | Yes | Yes | — |
| Framework-agnostic core as public API | Yes | Yes | Yes (core is framework-agnostic by design) |
| Undo/redo | Yes | No | No |
| Dependency footprint | Zero runtime dependencies | Zero | Zero (core) |

## Where this project genuinely leads

Cross-referencing the table above against `react-grid-layout`
specifically: magnetic snap-to-grid, visual alignment guides, the
blocked-move feedback event, named layout presets, grid-to-SVG export,
localizable ARIA strings, live-resyncing per-item `autoHeight`, and
multi-select with group move/resize all have no equivalent there. None
of these are exotic — they're the kind of real-world friction points a
dedicated roadmap process exists specifically to find and close one at
a time.

## Where this project is genuinely behind

- **Ecosystem size and battle-testing.** `react-grid-layout` has years
  more production usage across far more companies — not a feature gap
  this library can close by writing code, just a newer project.
- **Framework breadth.** `gridstack.js` covers Vue, React, and Angular
  from one core engine. This project ships genuinely separate Vue,
  React, and Angular packages rather than one universal wrapper — a
  different tradeoff, not strictly worse, but a real difference worth
  naming.
- **Sub-grids / nesting.** `gridstack.js` supports grids-within-grids as
  first-class nested structures. This project's cross-grid feature is
  sibling-to-sibling dragging between independent grid instances — a
  different capability, not a nesting system.
- **Swap-on-drag.** In `gridstack.js`'s default top-gravity mode,
  dragging one item onto another of the same size swaps their
  positions. This project only pushes items aside via compaction.

## Bottom line

Against a genuinely established incumbent like `react-grid-layout`,
this project's case rests on a meaningfully larger feature set —
several with no equivalent in `react-grid-layout` at all — at the cost
of being the newer, smaller-community option without the multi-year
production track record `react-grid-layout` can claim.
What keyboard and screen-reader support Keystone Dashboard Layout for React actually provides — and what it deliberately doesn't (yet).

Same scope and reasoning as the Vue port's own
[Accessibility scope](/vue/guide/project/accessibility/) — this page
documents this package's own implementation specifically, confirmed
directly against `GridItem.tsx`'s own source, not assumed from feature
parity claims alone.

## What's implemented

### Keyboard move and resize

Every non-static, editable `GridItem` is keyboard-focusable
(`tabIndex={0}`) and operable:

- **Arrow keys** move it by one grid unit, if it's draggable.
- **Shift + arrow keys** resize it by one grid unit, if it's resizable.

Each keypress is treated as a complete, atomic gesture — implemented as
a synthetic `dragstart` immediately followed by `dragend` (or
`resizestart`/`resizeend`), the same two calls a real mouse gesture's
start and release would produce, so `GridLayout`'s own compaction/
collision/`multiSelect` group-move handling applies identically
regardless of which input method triggered the change.

**Works with `multiSelect`'s group move/resize too** — arrow-key/
Shift+arrow movement on a focused, *selected* item moves/resizes every
other selected item by the same delta, the same as a mouse/touch drag
already does. See [Multi-select & group move/resize](/react/examples/multi-select-group-move-resize/).

**Deliberately scoped to single-unit steps**, not a full
[WAI-ARIA grid](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/grid/) or
[application](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/) widget pattern.
This library isn't a traditional data grid — it's a freeform draggable
canvas — so the full APG grid pattern doesn't map cleanly onto it.

### Screen reader support

- Each interactive item gets `role="group"` and
  `aria-roledescription` (default `"Draggable, resizable item"`), so a
  screen reader announces it as something other than a plain, silent
  `<div>`.
- `aria-describedby` points to a visually-hidden instructions string
  ("Press arrow keys to move." / "Press shift plus arrow keys to
  resize.", each only included if that action actually applies to the
  item) — discoverable on focus, not a mandatory upfront announcement.
- A visible focus outline, so a keyboard user can actually see which
  item currently has focus.

### A deliberate, non-obvious design decision worth calling out

Keyboard move/resize **ignores `dragAllowFrom`/`dragIgnoreFrom`/
`resizeIgnoreFrom`** entirely — confirmed directly in `handleKeyDown`,
which reads only `resolvedDraggable`/`resolvedResizable` and never
touches any of the three. Those fields restrict which DOM element a
*mouse* drag/resize gesture can originate from (see
[Drag allow/ignore elements](/react/examples/drag-allow-ignore-elements/)
and [Custom drag handle](/react/examples/custom-drag-handle-close-button/)),
which is a concept that doesn't map onto keyboard interaction at all. A
keyboard user who focuses the item gets full move/resize access
regardless of whether a mouse user is restricted to a specific handle —
intentional, matching the Vue port's own identical reasoning:
restricting keyboard users *further* than mouse users, just because a
mouse-specific UI affordance (a drag handle) exists, would be the wrong
direction for an accessibility feature to take.

### Localizable ARIA strings

The close button's label, `aria-roledescription`, and the keyboard
move/resize instructions are all overridable rather than hardcoded
English literals — see [Localizable ARIA strings](/react/examples/aria-labels/)
and [ARIA labels](/react/api/interfaces/aria-labels/).

## What's not covered (tracked, not silently ignored)

- **No roving-tabindex grid navigation.** Tabbing moves through items in
  DOM order, the same as any other focusable elements on a page —
  there's no arrow-key-based "move focus to the item above/below/left/
  right" navigation independent of actually moving the focused item.
- **No keyboard equivalent for the drag-from-outside / drag-between-grids
  examples** ([Drag, drop from outside](/react/examples/outside-drag-drop/),
  [Drag, drop from grid to grid](/react/examples/cross-grid-drag-drop/)) —
  those are consumer-level example code, not library internals.
- **Not independently audited against WCAG success criteria** or run
  through an automated tool (axe, Lighthouse, etc.).
- **Color contrast and the default item styling generally** haven't
  been reviewed — `GridItem`'s content is unstyled by default, so this
  is mostly a consumer responsibility.

## Verifying this

`GridItemKeyboard.spec.tsx` covers: focus attributes present/absent
correctly based on static/edit-mode state, arrow-key movement
(including bounds clamping and the `isDraggable: false` guard),
shift+arrow resize (including `minW`/`minH` clamping and the
`isResizable: false` guard), and that non-arrow keys and disabled
edit-mode are correctly no-ops.
How Keystone Dashboard Layout for React compares to Kendo TileLayout and DevExtreme's Dashboard Designer.

## Scope, and why this is separate from Comparison: alternatives

[Comparison: alternatives](/react/guide/project/comparison-alternatives/)
scopes itself to open-source peers in the same category. This page
covers two commercial products instead. Kendo's actual component is
called **TileLayout** (available for jQuery, Angular, React, and
Blazor) — and unlike the Vue port (which has no Kendo equivalent to
compare against at all, since Kendo doesn't ship a Vue build), this
package has a **real, direct competitor** here: Kendo does ship a React
build of TileLayout. DevExtreme's **Dashboard Designer** is a full BI
platform, not a standalone layout component — this page compares
against just its layout engine (the drag/resize/arrange mechanics),
since that's the only part in the same category as this library.

## The bigger architectural difference

Both commercial products use a **recursive binary split-pane tree**:
adding a new item splits the largest existing pane in half; resizing
means dragging the separator line between two adjacent panes, not
independent per-item resize handles. This library uses **freeform,
independent `x`/`y`/`w`/`h` grid coordinates** instead: any item can
move to any free position on its own, with its own resize handles on
its own edges. Neither approach is strictly better — a split-pane tree
structurally guarantees no overlaps and no compaction step, at the cost
of items never being fully independent of their neighbors; freeform
coordinates give full independent placement, at the cost of needing an
explicit collision/compaction system.

## Feature comparison

| Feature | This project | Kendo TileLayout | DevExtreme Dashboard (layout engine) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Layout model | Freeform x/y/w/h grid coordinates | CSS Grid, col/row/colSpan/rowSpan | Recursive binary split-pane tree |
| Resize any of 8 edges/corners independently | Yes | No — bottom/right edges + bottom-right corner only | No — drag the separator between two adjacent panes |
| Drag to an arbitrary free position | Yes | No — reorders within CSS Grid auto-flow | No — inserts into the tree at a new split point |
| Click-to-select, click-to-place reorder (no drag gesture) | No | **Yes** — a real, non-drag accessibility alternative worth considering here | No |
| React support | Native, ground-up | Yes — a real, direct competitor here | Via a wrapper layer over a shared core |
| Licensing | MIT, free | Commercial, but free for the React build specifically | Commercial, no free tier |
| Cross-grid drag/drop between independent instances | Yes | No | No |
| Drag-and-drop from outside the component | Yes | No | No — Toolbox is click-to-add, not a drag gesture |
| Responsive breakpoints | Yes | No | Auto-stretches to fit its container — a different, non-breakpoint mechanism |
| Undo/redo | Yes | No | No — dashboard-level save/reload only |
| Multi-select group move/resize | Yes | No | No — single-item drag only |
| Magnetic snap-to-grid / alignment guides | Yes (both) | No | No |
| Keyboard move/resize | Yes | Comparable, via Ctrl+arrow (resize) / Shift+arrow (reorder) | Not documented as a distinct mode |
| Per-item lock against rearrangement | Yes (`isStatic`) | Yes | Closer to a dashboard-level view mode than a per-item flag |
| **Maximize/restore an item to fill the surface** | **No — a real, confirmed gap** | No | **Yes** |
| Save/restore layout state | Yes | Yes — comparable | Yes — comparable |
| Export layout as image/SVG | Yes, dependency-free | No | Yes, but exports the dashboard's data visualizations, not a plain layout-shell export |
| Data source binding, drill-down, BI charting | **Out of scope entirely — a deliberate boundary** | No (presentation-only, same category as this library) | **Yes — its entire reason to exist** |

## Honest summary

Against **Kendo TileLayout**: unlike the Vue port (which has no Kendo
React/Vue build to compare against directly), this is a genuine,
direct competitor for React consumers specifically — and this library
is ahead on nearly every drag/resize/layout-mechanics dimension: full
8-edge independent resize vs. a 3-handle/axis-restricted model,
freeform positioning vs. reorder-only, cross-grid drag, outside drop,
snap/alignment guides, undo/redo, multi-select. TileLayout's genuine
advantages: being one component in a large commercial suite with paid
support, a mature click-move-click accessibility mode this library
doesn't have, and being free for the React build specifically.

Against **DevExtreme Dashboard**: these aren't real competitors for
most consumers — Dashboard Designer is a BI-authoring product where
drag/resize layout is one supporting piece of a much larger
data-analytics platform. The one genuine, worth-tracking gap even at
the pure layout-mechanics level is **maximize/restore** — tracked on
the [Roadmap](/react/guide/project/roadmap/), not yet designed.

## What's not worth chasing from either

- **Kendo's CSS Grid-based, resize-restricted-to-3-handles model** —
  adopting this would be a regression, not a gap to close.
- **DevExtreme's recursive split-pane structure itself** — rebuilding
  around that architecture would abandon the freeform positioning model
  that's core to what this library is.
- **DevExtreme's BI/data-analytics layer entirely** — a different
  product category by design.

## Unit & component tests — Vitest + React Testing Library

Pure-function tests for the grid math live in `keystone-dashboard-layout-core`
(shared with the Vue port). This package's own tests cover `GridLayout`,
`GridItem`, `GridItemDragHandle`, `GridItemCloseButton`, and every
exported hook (`useLayoutStorage`, `useLayoutPresets`,
`useCrossGridDrag`, `useGridItemDrag`, `useGridItemResize`), rendered
via React Testing Library against jsdom.

```sh
pnpm test            # watch mode
pnpm test:ui         # Vitest UI
pnpm test:coverage   # single run with coverage
pnpm test:mutation   # mutation tests (Stryker)
```

### Coverage gate

A **90% minimum** (lines, statements, functions, branches) is enforced
over the library's own source — the same gate the Vue port uses.
Excluded: pure type-declaration files (no emitted JS to cover), the
package's own public barrel (`src/index.ts` — a genuine "does the
barrel actually export what it claims" check belongs to a
pack-and-install smoke test, not unit-test line coverage), and test
infrastructure (`__tests__/test-helpers.ts`).

### Component testing approach

`GridLayout` and `GridItem` are tested together, rendering a real
`GridLayout` with real `GridItem` children — the same shape actual
usage takes, so the Context contract (see
[Architecture](/react/guide/project/architecture/)) behaves exactly as
it does in production, rather than relying on a hand-rolled fake
provider value.

A few things need mocking, since jsdom can't provide them:

- **`ResizeObserver`** — jsdom doesn't implement it at all. Replaced
  with a stub for most tests; the initial container-width measurement
  is handled separately.
- **The native drag/resize engine's own pointer handling** — real,
  trusted pointer events and native layout aren't something jsdom can
  produce faithfully. Tests invoke the component's actual drag/resize
  handling logic directly, rather than trying to simulate a full, real
  mouse gesture through jsdom.

## End-to-end tests — Playwright

Browser tests that drive real drag/resize/responsive interactions
against a real demo app, across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit —
matching the Vue port's own e2e setup and coverage shape.

```sh

npm run test:e2e          # headless, all three browser engines
npm run test:e2e:ui       # interactive UI mode, good for writing new tests
npm run test:e2e:report   # open the HTML report from the last run
```

steps → up) rather than clicking a locator, since the native engine
needs a real sequence of pointer events to recognize a drag/resize

underlying native engine, as the Vue port's own e2e tests.

```ts
interface ICompactor {
  readonly type: string;
  compact(layout: TLayout, cols: number, context: ICompactorContext): TLayout;
}
```

| Member | Description |
|---|---|
| `type` | A short, descriptive name for this strategy — informational only (e.g. for logging); never read by `GridLayout` itself. |
| `compact(layout, cols, context)` | Compacts a layout, **returning a new array** — must not mutate the input `layout` or any of its items in place. |

## `ICompactorContext`

```ts
interface ICompactorContext {
  compactType: ECompactType;
  minPositions?: Record<string | number, { x?: number; y?: number }>;
}
```

| Field | Description |
|---|---|
| `compactType` | Which built-in strategy currently applies — informational, read from `GridLayout`'s own `compactType` prop at the moment compaction runs. A custom compactor decides for itself whether/how to use this; nothing enforces it. |
| `minPositions` | Present only during a `restoreOnDrag`-gated compaction (drag end) — the pre-drag position each item shouldn't rise/shift any tighter than. Absent for every other trigger (resize end, add/remove, mount, breakpoint change, `compactNow()`/`rearrange()`), and for the two `*_OVERLAP` types. |

## The five built-in strategies

Exported individually, as a starting point for a custom compactor to
delegate back to for part of a layout (e.g. compact everything except
one pinned row) rather than reimplementing standard compaction from
scratch:

```ts
import {
  verticalCompactor,
  horizontalCompactor,
  noCompactor,
  verticalOverlapCompactor,
  horizontalOverlapCompactor,
  getCompactor,
} from 'keystone-dashboard-layout-vue';
```

| Export | Backs |
|---|---|
| `verticalCompactor` | `ECompactType.VERTICAL` (the default) |
| `horizontalCompactor` | `ECompactType.HORIZONTAL` |
| `noCompactor` | `ECompactType.NONE` |
| `verticalOverlapCompactor` | `ECompactType.VERTICAL_OVERLAP` |
| `horizontalOverlapCompactor` | `ECompactType.HORIZONTAL_OVERLAP` |
| `getCompactor(compactType)` | Looks up the built-in `ICompactor` matching a given `ECompactType` — the same mapping `GridLayout` itself uses internally when the `compactor` prop isn't set. |

See [Pluggable compaction](/vue/examples/pluggable-compaction/) for a
full working custom compactor, and [ECompactType](/vue/api/enums/compact-type/)
for what each built-in strategy actually does.
The typed payloads for GridLayout's cross-grid and outside-drop events.
The payload shape carried on GridLayout and GridItem's internal eventBus.
Types for values reachable through a GridLayout/GridItem instance ref via defineExpose.
serializeLayout/deserializeLayout, useLayoutStorage, and useLayoutPresets — the exported building blocks and composables behind saving and loading a layout.

One entry in a `GridLayout`'s `layout` array. The optional fields mirror
the corresponding `GridItem` props (`isDraggable`, `minH`, etc.) —
Vue's own `GridItem` takes most of these as direct component props
rather than reading them from the layout item, so setting one here is
mainly useful for configuring items from data instead of template props.

```ts
interface ILayoutItemRequired {
  i: string | number;
  h: number;
  w: number;
  x: number;
  y: number;
}

interface ILayoutItem<TMeta = unknown> extends ILayoutItemRequired {
  // ...optional fields below
}
```

`ILayoutItemRequired` is exported separately too, in case you need to
type just the required fields on their own (a minimal seed object before
optional fields are added, say).

## Required fields

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `i` | `string \| number` | Unique identifier, matched against a `GridItem`'s `i` prop. Must be either a non-empty string or a finite number — never both at once, and never an empty string. String matching against a `GridItem`'s own `i` prop is case-insensitive (`'Widget-1'` matches `'widget-1'`); number matching is exact. |
| `h` | `number` | Height, in grid row units. |
| `w` | `number` | Width, in grid column units. |
| `x` | `number` | Horizontal position, in grid column units. |
| `y` | `number` | Vertical position, in grid row units. |

## Optional fields

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `isDraggable` | `boolean` | Per-item drag override. |
| `isResizable` | `boolean` | Per-item resize override. |
| `isStatic` | `boolean` | Excludes this item from dragging, resizing, and collision cascades. |
| `maxH` / `maxW` / `minH` / `minW` | `number` | Per-item size constraints. |
| `zIndex` | `number \| null` | CSS `z-index` override, winning over the static/dragging/resizing CSS-class defaults. |
| `showCloseButton` | `boolean` | Per-item override; `undefined` defers to the grid-wide default. |
| `autoScroll` | `boolean` | Per-item override for native auto-scroll near a container edge during drag/resize. |
| `preserveAspectRatio` | `boolean` | Per-item override for locking width/height ratio while resizing. |
| `ariaLabels` | `IGridAriaLabels` | Per-item override, merged over the grid-wide `ariaLabels` prop and the built-in English defaults. |
| `dragAllowFrom` / `dragIgnoreFrom` | `string \| null` | CSS selectors restricting where a drag can/can't start. |
| `resizeIgnoreFrom` | `string \| null` | CSS selector for elements that shouldn't start a resize. |
| `dragActivationDistance` | `TDragActivationDistance \| null` | Minimum pointer movement, in pixels, before a pointerdown counts as a drag — one value for every pointer type, or distinct values per mouse/touch/pen. |
| `isBounded` | `boolean \| null` | Per-item override for restricting dragging to within the container. |
| `resizeHandles` | `TResizeHandle[] \| null` | Restricts which of the 8 resize-hint spans render/activate for this item. An empty array is a valid "no handle-driven resize" value, distinct from `isResizable: false`. |
| `isMirrored` | `boolean` | Whether this item participates in the grid's own RTL mirroring. Default `true`. |
| `enableEditMode` | `boolean` | Per-item override for the master interactivity switch. |
| `borderRadiusPx` / `useBorderRadius` | `number` / `boolean` | Per-item border radius override. |
| `showResizeHandles` / `resizeHandleColor` | `boolean` / `string` | Per-item visible resize-handle override. |
| `autoHeight` | `boolean` | Re-runs this item's own size measurement whenever its rendered content changes size. No grid-wide equivalent. |
| `moved` | `boolean` | Set internally by compaction/collision helpers to short-circuit infinite loops — not meant to be set by consumers. |
| `data` | `TMeta` | Optional, consumer-defined payload — never read or written by the library itself. Round-trips through serialize/deserialize like any other field, as long as it's JSON-serializable. |

## `TMeta` — attaching typed data to a layout item

```ts
interface IWidgetConfig {
  chartType: 'bar' | 'line';
}

const layout = ref<TLayout<IWidgetConfig>>([
  { h: 2, i: '0', w: 2, x: 0, y: 0, data: { chartType: 'bar' } },
]);
```

Attach whatever payload an item needs directly on the layout item,
instead of maintaining a parallel array keyed by `i` to look it up
separately. Every existing usage of `ILayoutItem`/`TLayout` without a
type argument keeps working unchanged — the default (`unknown`) only
matters if you actually read `.data` and want it typed as something
more specific.

## `TLayoutItem`

Structurally identical to `ILayoutItem`. Both exist in the codebase;
prefer `ILayoutItem` for new code — `TLayoutItem` is kept for backwards
compatibility with existing type annotations.
exportLayoutAsSvg and readOutsideDropPayload — two standalone utility functions exported from the package root.

## `exportLayoutAsSvg`

```ts
function exportLayoutAsSvg(layout: TLayout, options?: IExportLayoutAsSvgOptions): string;
```

```ts
interface IExportLayoutAsSvgOptions {
  colNum?: number;          // default: 12
  rowHeight?: number;       // default: 150
  margin?: [number, number]; // default: [10, 10]
  containerWidth?: number;  // default: 1200 — must be supplied explicitly; see note below
  itemFill?: string;        // default: '#eef2ff'
  itemStroke?: string;      // default: '#c7d2fe'
  labelColor?: string;      // default: '#3730a3'
  backgroundColor?: string | null; // default: null (transparent)
}
```

Renders a `TLayout` as a standalone SVG string, each item drawn as a
labeled rectangle from the layout data alone — not a snapshot of
whatever's actually rendered inside each `GridItem`. Good for a
structural thumbnail of the layout itself, not a substitute for a real
screenshot of custom slot content. Never throws: an empty layout
produces a valid, empty SVG.

`containerWidth` has to be passed explicitly, unlike `GridLayout`
itself, which measures its own container automatically — there's no
DOM element for this standalone function to measure. Pass the same
width your actual grid renders at for a matching result.

The returned string is a complete `<svg>...</svg>` document — usable
directly, downloaded as a `.svg` file via a `Blob`, or drawn onto a
`<canvas>` first if a raster PNG/JPEG is specifically needed. See
[Export layout as SVG](/vue/examples/svg-export/) for a full example.

## `readOutsideDropPayload`

```ts
function readOutsideDropPayload<T>(
  dataTransfer: DataTransfer | null | undefined,
  mimeType?: string, // default: 'text/plain'
): T | null;
```

Reads and JSON-parses a native `DataTransfer` payload by MIME type —
every consumer of `allowOutsideDrop`'s `item-dropped-from-outside`
event otherwise re-implements the same `dataTransfer.getData(mimeType)`/
`JSON.parse` parsing by hand. Never throws: a missing MIME type or
malformed JSON both return `null`. Performs no runtime shape validation
against `T` — that's the caller's own responsibility, since the payload
is whatever the consumer's own drag source chose to attach.

:::caution[A real gotcha with native drag-and-drop]
`dataTransfer.getData()` only returns real values during the `drop`
event itself — not `dragenter`/`dragover`.
:::

See [outsideDropAccept & readOutsideDropPayload](/vue/examples/outside-drop-accept-payload/)
for a full working example.
The internal event bus GridLayout and GridItem use to talk to each other.

`GridLayout` and every `GridItem` communicate through a shared,
named-event bus — `GridLayout` creates it (via an in-house
`createEventEmitter()` helper, not a third-party library) and provides
it; every `GridItem` injects it. This is internal plumbing, not part of
the public component API, but understanding it helps when debugging why
a prop change on `GridLayout` did or didn't reach an item.

:::tip[Most consumers never need this page]
Everything here happens automatically based on the props/events already
documented for [GridLayout](/vue/components/grid-layout/props/) and
[GridItem](/vue/components/grid-item/props/). This page exists for anyone
digging into the library's internals or filing a detailed bug report.
:::

## GridLayout → GridItem

Pushed down whenever the corresponding `GridLayout` prop changes, so
every item can react without `GridLayout` needing to re-render each one
individually.

| Message | Payload | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `changeDirection` | `boolean` (isMirrored) | RTL toggle. |
| `compact` | — | "Recompute your style, something upstream changed." |
| `setBounded` | `boolean` | Cascades `isBounded` — only applied by items whose own `isBounded` prop is `null`. |
| `setBorderRadiusPx` | `number` | Cascades `borderRadiusPx` — only applied when the item's own prop is `null`. |
| `setColNum` | `number` | Cascades the resolved column count. |
| `setDraggable` | `boolean` | Cascades `isDraggable` — only applied when the item's own prop is `null`. |
| `setEnableEditMode` | `boolean` | Cascades `enableEditMode` — only applied when the item's own prop is `null`. |
| `setMargin` | `number[]` | Cascades `[horizontal, vertical]` margin. |
| `setMaxRows` | `number` | Cascades `maxRows`. |
| `setResizable` | `boolean` | Cascades `isResizable` — only applied when the item's own prop is `null`. |
| `setResizeHandles` | `TResizeHandle[]` | Cascades the default resize-hint span set — only applied when the item's own `resizeHandles` prop is `null`. |
| `setRowHeight` | `number` | Cascades `rowHeight`. |
| `setShowCloseButton` | `boolean` | Cascades `showCloseButton` — only applied by items whose own prop is `null`. |
| `setTransformScale` | `number` | Cascades `transformScale`. |
| `setUseBorderRadius` | `boolean` | Cascades `useBorderRadius` — only applied when the item's own prop is `null`. |
| `setUseCssTransforms` | `boolean` | Cascades `useCssTransforms` — applied unconditionally to every item (no per-item override exists for this one). |
| `updateWidth` | `number` | Cascades the container's measured (or min/maxW-adjusted effective) pixel width. |

## GridItem → GridLayout

An item reporting its own drag/resize progress, or a genuine click, up
to the parent.

| Message | Payload | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `dragEvent` | `IEventsData` | A drag is starting, in progress, or ending — lets `GridLayout` resolve collisions against every *other* item and update the drag placeholder. |
| `resizeEvent` | `IEventsData` | Same, for a resize. |
| `itemClicked` | `IItemClickedData` | A genuine click/tap (drag/resize trailing clicks already suppressed) — backs `GridLayout`'s own `multiSelect` selection handling. |

See [Architecture](/vue/guide/project/architecture/) for the full
internal picture, including why `$parent` access (not props) is used
for the initial state a `GridItem` reads at mount.
Every prop GridLayout accepts, with defaults and links to live examples.

Only `layout` is required — everything else has a default. Most
boolean/number props here have a matching prop on [`GridItem`](/vue/components/grid-item/props/)
that can override it per-item; see each prop's note.

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `layout` | `TLayout` (required) | — | The layout array — one entry per `GridItem` rendered in the default slot, matched by `i`. See [Layout types](/vue/api/types/layout/). |
| `autoSize` | `boolean` | `true` | Deprecated — prefer `heightMode`. Grows/shrinks the container's height to fit the layout's content. Ignored once `heightMode` is set explicitly. |
| `heightMode` | `'auto' \| 'fixed' \| 'scroll' \| 'fit' \| null` | `null` | How the container's height is determined. `null` defers to `autoSize` (no behavior change for existing consumers). `'auto'`: grows/shrinks to fit content — today's `autoSize: true`. `'fixed'`: no explicit height applied — today's `autoSize: false`. `'scroll'`: same as `'fixed'`, but adds `overflow-y: auto` so tall content scrolls internally. `'fit'`: height locked to `100%` of the parent, with the same `overflow-y: auto` as `'scroll'` — for filling a fixed-size panel and scrolling its own content. |
| `ariaLabels` | `IGridAriaLabels` | `{}` | Grid-wide overrides for localizable UI/ARIA strings — the close button's visually-hidden label, keyboard move/resize instructions, and the item's `aria-roledescription`. Only the keys actually set here override the built-in English defaults; a specific `GridItem` can further override any of these for just itself via its own `ariaLabels` prop. See [Localizable ARIA strings](/vue/examples/aria-labels/). |
| `allowCrossGridDrag` | `boolean` | `false` | Lets this grid's items be dragged into any other `GridLayout` that also has this set, and (unless `disableExternalDrop` is set) accept drops from them. **Must be set on both the source and the target grid** — a drop onto a grid that doesn't have this set is indistinguishable from dropping on empty space. See [Drag, drop from grid to grid](/vue/examples/cross-grid-drag-drop/) and [Cross-grid drop restrictions](/vue/examples/cross-grid-drop-restrictions/). |
| `disableExternalDrop` | `boolean` | `false` | When `true`, this grid never accepts an incoming cross-grid drop — its own items can still be dragged *out* to other grids if `allowCrossGridDrag` is set, but nothing can be dropped *into* it. Has no effect if `allowCrossGridDrag` is `false`. |
| `layoutId` | `string` | auto-generated | A stable identifier for this grid, used in cross-grid event payloads to say which grid an item came from or was rejected by. Only meaningful with `allowCrossGridDrag`. |
| `allowOutsideDrop` | `boolean` | `false` | Accepts native HTML5 drag-and-drop from *outside* the grid system entirely — a plain `draggable="true"` element that's neither a `GridItem` nor another `GridLayout`. Distinct from `allowCrossGridDrag`/`disableExternalDrop`, which are both about dragging *between* grids. See [Drag, drop from outside](/vue/examples/outside-drag-drop/) and [into multiple grids](/vue/examples/outside-drag-drop-multiple-grids/). |
| `outsideDropWidth` | `number` | `2` | Width, in grid columns, of the live placeholder. Ignored when `allowOutsideDrop` is `false`. |
| `outsideDropHeight` | `number` | `2` | Height, in grid rows, of the live placeholder. Ignored when `allowOutsideDrop` is `false`. |
| `outsideDropAccept` | `((dataTransfer: DataTransfer \| null) => boolean) \| null` | `null` | A predicate rejecting incompatible native drags before the placeholder appears. `null` accepts everything. See [outsideDropAccept & readOutsideDropPayload](/vue/examples/outside-drop-accept-payload/). |
| `borderRadiusPx` | `number` | `10` | Border radius, in pixels, applied when `useBorderRadius` is on — cascades to every `GridItem` that doesn't set its own. See [Border radius](/vue/examples/border-radius/). |
| `breakpoints` | `IBreakpoints` | `{ xxl: 1600, xl: 1400, lg: 1200, md: 996, sm: 768, xs: 480, xxs: 0 }` | Container-width thresholds per breakpoint, used when `responsive` is enabled. |
| `colNum` | `number` | `12` | Maximum number of columns — caps whatever `cols`/breakpoint resolution would otherwise produce. |
| `cols` | `IColumns` | `{ xxl: 12, xl: 12, lg: 12, md: 10, sm: 6, xs: 4, xxs: 2 }` | Column count per breakpoint, used when `responsive` is true. |
| `compactor` | `ICompactor \| null` | `null` | Replaces the built-in compaction algorithm entirely — `null` keeps whichever built-in strategy `compactType` selects. See [Pluggable compaction](/vue/examples/pluggable-compaction/). |
| `compactType` | `ECompactType` | `ECompactType.VERTICAL` | Selects one of five built-in compaction strategies: `VERTICAL`, `HORIZONTAL`, `NONE`, `VERTICAL_OVERLAP`/`HORIZONTAL_OVERLAP`. See [Pluggable compaction](/vue/examples/pluggable-compaction/). |
| `distributeEvenly` | `boolean` | `false` | Spread items that would overflow the right edge evenly across available columns, instead of just clamping. See [Layout bounds & rendering options](/vue/examples/layout-bounds-rendering-options/). |
| `horizontalShift` | `boolean` | `false` | Push colliding items left/right instead of down, during an active drag/resize. See [Horizontal shift](/vue/examples/horizontal-shift/). |
| `isBounded` | `boolean` | `false` | Default `isBounded` for items that don't set their own. |
| `isDraggable` | `boolean` | `true` | Default `isDraggable` for items that don't set their own. |
| `isMirrored` | `boolean` | `false` | Enables RTL layout mirroring. See [Mirrored (RTL)](/vue/examples/mirrored-rtl/). |
| `isResizable` | `boolean` | `true` | Default `isResizable` for items that don't set their own. |
| `margin` | `number[]` | `[10, 10]` | `[horizontal, vertical]` spacing between items, in pixels. |
| `maxRows` | `number` | `Infinity` | Maximum number of rows the layout may grow to. See [Layout bounds & rendering options](/vue/examples/layout-bounds-rendering-options/). |
| `multiSelect` | `boolean` | `false` | Opt-in multi-select and group move/resize. See [Multi-select & group move/resize](/vue/examples/multi-select-group-move-resize/). |
| `enableEditMode` | `boolean` | `true` | Grid-wide default for `enableEditMode` on every `GridItem` that doesn't set its own. See [Edit mode toggle](/vue/examples/edit-mode-toggle/). |
| `enableUndoRedo` | `boolean` | `false` | Opts into `undo()`/`redo()` history, at committed-change granularity. See [Undo/redo](/vue/examples/undo-redo/). |
| `preventCollision` | `boolean` | `false` | Block a drag/resize that would collide, instead of pushing the other item. See [Prevent collision](/vue/examples/prevent-collision/). |
| `responsive` | `boolean` | `false` | Enables breakpoint switching. See [Responsive breakpoints](/vue/examples/responsive-breakpoints/). |
| `responsiveLayouts` | `TResponsiveLayout` | `{}` | Pre-defined layouts per breakpoint, instead of auto-generating one. See [Responsive predefined layouts](/vue/examples/responsive-predefined-layouts/). |
| `restoreOnDrag` | `boolean` | `false` | While dragging, don't let other items compact past their pre-drag position until the drag ends. |
| `rowHeight` | `number` | `150` | Height of one grid row, in pixels. |
| `showCloseButton` | `boolean` | `false` | Default `showCloseButton` for items that don't set their own. See [Show close button](/vue/examples/close-button/). |
| `showGridLines` | `boolean` | `false` | Renders visible grid line guides behind the items. See [Show grid lines](/vue/examples/grid-lines/). |
| `showAlignmentGuides` | `boolean` | `false` | Shows Figma-style alignment guide lines while dragging or resizing. See [Alignment guides while dragging](/vue/examples/alignment-guides/). |

| `useCssTransforms` | `boolean` | `true` | Position items via CSS `transform` instead of `top`/`left`. |
| `undoHistoryLimit` | `number` | `50` | Caps how many snapshots `undo()` can step back through when `enableUndoRedo` is on. See [Undo/redo](/vue/examples/undo-redo/). |

The default slot and the custom drag-placeholder slot GridLayout exposes.

## Default slot Where every `GridItem` you render goes. `GridLayout` itself doesn't create or manage `GridItem` instances — you render one per layout entry yourself, typically with `v-for`: ```vue Item {{ item.i }} ``` ## `#placeholder` Customizes the drag placeholder's content — the box shown while an item is being dragged or resized, indicating where it will land. By default this is a plain colored box with nothing inside it. Content you provide here renders inside the same internal `GridItem` the library already uses for the placeholder, layered on top of its existing background/sizing rather than replacing it. ```vue ... ``` The slot receives two scope props: | Prop | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | `placeholder` | `{ x, y, w, h }` | The placeholder's current grid position/size — updates live as you drag or resize. | | `isDragging` | `boolean` | Whether a drag or resize is currently in progress. | Visibility is still controlled by the library — your slot content is present in the DOM regardless of whether a drag is actually happening; you only control what's rendered *inside* the placeholder, not when it's shown. See [Custom drag-placeholder content](/vue/examples/custom-drag-placeholder/) for a full example.
Adding keystone-dashboard-layout-core directly, and how to reach the extra cross-grid-registry subpath export.

```sh
npm i keystone-dashboard-layout-core
```

Works with `import`, `require`, and TypeScript's own type resolution —
the package ships ESM, CJS, and its own `.d.ts` types, so no extra
`@types` package is needed either way.

```ts
import { collides, compactLayout, getBreakpointFromWidth } from 'keystone-dashboard-layout-core';
```

## The cross-grid-registry subpath

Everything above comes from the package's own main entry point. One
piece is deliberately **not** re-exported there: the cross-grid
registry — the runtime coordination point multiple grids on the same
page use to recognize each other for drag-and-drop between them. It's
a stateful, singleton-style module tied to component mount/unmount,
not a pure calculation the way everything else here is, so it's kept
as its own, explicit subpath import instead of bundled into the main
one:

```ts
import { registerCrossGridZone } from 'keystone-dashboard-layout-core/gridlayout/helpers/cross-grid-registry';
import type { ICrossGridZone } from 'keystone-dashboard-layout-core/gridlayout/interfaces/cross-grid.interfaces';
```

Only worth reaching for directly if you're building a new framework
integration from scratch — the Vue and React packages already wire this
up internally for their own `allowCrossGridDrag` prop.

| Event | Payload | When |

| `cross-grid-item-dropped` | `({ item, sourceLayoutId })`, typed `ICrossGridItemDropped` | Fired on the *target* grid when an item is successfully moved into it from another grid. See [Drag, drop from grid to grid](/vue/examples/cross-grid-drag-drop/). |

| `dragstart` | `(id: number)` | A drag begins. |
| `layout-ready` | `(layout: TLayout)` | Fired once, after the container's width is known and every item's size is stable — the first reliable point to inspect final positions/sizes. |
| `layout-updated` | `(layout: TLayout)` | Fired once during mount (after initial compaction), and again after every subsequent layout mutation — drag/resize completion, item add/remove, align/distribute, undo/redo. |
| `move-blocked-by-collision` | `(id: string \| number)` | Fired when `preventCollision` blocks a drag or resize. See [Blocked-move feedback](/vue/examples/blocked-move-feedback/). |
| `selection-changed` | `(selectedItems: (string \| number)[])` | Fired whenever the current `multiSelect` selection changes. See [Multi-select & group move/resize](/vue/examples/multi-select-group-move-resize/). |

[`EGridLayoutEvent`](/vue/api/enums/grid-layout-events/) for the enum
backing these event names.

:::note[Payloads aren't compile-time checked]
The payload shapes in the table above are accurate for what's actually
emitted, but `GridLayout`'s own emit declaration doesn't statically
type the payload arguments — only the event *names* are checked by

`EGridLayoutEvent.CHANGED_DIRECTION` and `CONTAINER_RESIZED` exist on the

listening for `@changed-direction`/`@container-resized` on `GridLayout`
won't see anything fire. See [Roadmap](/vue/guide/project/roadmap/).

What keystone-dashboard-layout-core is, who it's for, and how it relates to the Vue/React/Angular packages.

`keystone-dashboard-layout-core` is the shared implementation
underneath every framework package in this project. Collision
detection, bin-packing, compaction, responsive breakpoint resolution,
alignment guides, and more all live here exactly once — the Vue, React,
and Angular packages each call into this same code rather than
maintaining their own copies of the hard, easy-to-get-subtly-wrong
parts of a drag-and-drop grid.

## Who this is for

Most people don't need this page at all — installing
**[Vue](/vue/)**, **[React](/react/)**, or **[Angular](/angular/)**
already pulls this in as a dependency, and none of its exports need to
be touched directly to use any of those three packages normally.

This package is worth installing and using **directly** when you want
the same algorithms *without* any of those three components — for
example:

- Validating a layout array (bounds, key uniqueness, margin/breakpoint
  shape) on a server, before it ever reaches a browser.
- Computing compaction or collision resolution for a batch job — a
  script that rearranges saved dashboard layouts in bulk, say — with no
  UI involved at all.
- Building an integration for a framework this project doesn't ship a
  package for (Svelte, Solid, a plain web component, or anything else)
  — the same drag/resize engine, breakpoint logic, and layout math the
  three existing packages use, without reimplementing any of it.

## What's genuinely framework-free, and what isn't

The large majority of this package's own exports are pure functions:
plain data in, plain data out, no live DOM or component lifecycle
required at all. That covers collision detection, bin-packing,
compaction (all five built-in strategies), pixel-to-grid-unit math,
alignment-guide/snap calculation, multi-select align/distribute/range
commands, responsive breakpoint resolution, layout serialization, SVG
export, and every validator.

One deliberate exception: `createNativeDraggable`, `createNativeResizable`,
and `createNativeAutoScroll` (the native, Pointer Events-based
drag/resize engine both the Vue and React packages share) need a real
DOM to do anything at all — they attach real event listeners to real
elements. They're framework-*agnostic* (no Vue or React-specific code
whatsoever) but not DOM-*free*, unlike everything else this package
exports.

The CSS classes GridItem's root element conditionally applies.

`GridItem`'s root element always has the class `vue-grid-item`, plus a
combination of the conditional classes below depending on its current
state. Target these directly, after the library's stylesheet is loaded:

```css
/* After importing 'keystone-dashboard-layout-vue/style.css' */
.vue-grid-item {
  background: #1e293b;
  color: white;
}
```

## Conditional classes

| Class | Applied when |
|---|---|
| `css-transforms` | `useCssTransforms` is true (the default) — positioned via CSS `transform` instead of `top`/`left`. |
| `disable-userselect` | A drag is in progress. **Note:** the stylesheet's own rule for this is actually named `.disable-user-select` (with a hyphen between "user" and "select") — a real, confirmed mismatch in the library's own source between the class the component applies and the class its stylesheet defines, so this specific rule never actually matches anything applied at runtime. Text selection during drag isn't currently prevented by this mechanism as a result. |
| `no-touch` | On Android, when the item is draggable or resizable — overrides default touch handling so drag/resize gestures work correctly. |
| `render-rtl` | The item is currently rendering right-to-left. See [Mirrored (RTL)](/vue/examples/mirrored-rtl/). |
| `resizing` | A resize is in progress. |
| `vue-draggable` | The item is currently draggable (resolved from its own prop or the parent layout's default), not static, and edit mode is on. |
| `vue-draggable-dragging` | A drag is in progress (same condition as `disable-userselect`). |
| `vue-grid-item-has-header` | The `#header` slot is actually provided — switches to a vertical flex layout splitting header/body. See [GridItem slots](/vue/components/grid-item/slots/). |
| `vue-grid-item-selected` | The item is part of the current `multiSelect` selection. See [Multi-select & group move/resize](/vue/examples/multi-select-group-move-resize/). |
| `vue-resizable` | The item is currently resizable, not static, and edit mode is on. |
| `vue-static` | `isStatic` is true. See [Static items](/vue/examples/static-items/). |
| `vue-use-radius` | `useBorderRadius` is true. See [Border radius](/vue/examples/border-radius/). |

## The close button

Rendered internally as a `<button class="btn-close">` when
`showCloseButton && enableEditMode && !isStatic`. Style it directly:

```css
.vue-grid-item .btn-close {
  background: #ef4444;
}
```

...or replace it entirely with your own — see
[Custom drag handle & close button](/vue/examples/custom-drag-handle-close-button/),
which uses the library's own exported `CustomCloseButton` component
instead of the built-in button.

## Border radius

Set via an inline style (not a class) computed from the `borderRadiusPx`
prop, applied whenever `useBorderRadius` is true — see
[GridItem props](/vue/components/grid-item/props/) and
[Styling → Variables](/vue/components/styling/css-variables/) for the
SCSS-level default that applies when you don't set `borderRadiusPx`
yourself.
The CSS classes GridLayout's root element uses.

`GridLayout`'s root element gets the class `vue-grid-layout`. It's
`position: relative` with a 200ms `height` transition (so `autoSize`
changes animate smoothly) — override either directly:

```css
.vue-grid-layout {
  background: #0f172a;
}
```

## `.grid` — grid line guides

When `showGridLines` is enabled, `GridLayout` adds a `grid` class and
renders the guide lines via a `::before` pseudo-element, colored by the
`--grid-line-color` CSS custom property (a real, runtime-overridable
property — not a SCSS variable; see [Styling → Variables](/vue/components/styling/css-variables/)
for why that distinction matters here specifically).
See [Show grid lines](/vue/examples/grid-lines/) for a live demo.

## `.vue-grid-layout--active-drag`

Applied only while a cross-grid drag (`allowCrossGridDrag`) is in
progress, bumping this grid's own `z-index` to `1` — a real fix for a
real bug: with every grid establishing its own CSS stacking context
(`isolation: isolate`, needed separately so a negative-`z-index` static
item doesn't escape its own grid's subtree), a dragged item paints
behind whichever sibling grid happens to come later in the DOM, unless
its own source grid's stacking context is temporarily raised above its
siblings during the drag. Not meant to be restyled — documented here so
an unexpectedly-elevated `z-index` during a cross-grid drag isn't a
mystery if you notice it in devtools.

## `.vue-grid-alignment-guide` / `.vue-grid-spacing-indicator`

Rendered while `showAlignmentGuides`/`showSpacingGuides` are
respectively on, positioned absolutely as thin lines (`vue-grid-alignment-guide`)
or small labeled badges (`vue-grid-spacing-indicator`, e.g. "2 cols").
Style them directly:

```css
.vue-grid-alignment-guide {
  background: #f59e0b;
}
.vue-grid-spacing-indicator {
  background: #1e293b;
}
```

See [Alignment guides while dragging](/vue/examples/alignment-guides/)
for a live demo.

## `.vue-grid-placeholder`

The internal drag placeholder — a hidden `GridItem` shown only while
`isDragging` is true, marking where the dragged/resized item would
land. Style it to make the "drop target" more or less visually
prominent:

```css
.vue-grid-placeholder {
  background: rgba(59, 130, 246, 0.3);
}
```

## Sizing

`GridLayout`'s height is governed by `heightMode` (the modern prop) or
`autoSize` (the older, still-supported alias) — see
[GridLayout props](/vue/components/grid-layout/props/) for the full set
of modes, including `'scroll'`/`'fit'`, which also apply an inline
`overflow-y: auto`. There's no dedicated class for any of this; it's
applied as inline styles.

:::caution[These are SCSS variables, not CSS custom properties]
Everything on this page is a compile-time SCSS `$variable`, baked into
the published stylesheet at build time — **not** a runtime-overridable
`--css-custom-property`. You can't change these from your own
stylesheet the way you would a `:root { --foo: red; }` override. To
customize them, override the resulting classes directly (see
[Styling → GridItem](/vue/components/styling/css-grid-item/) and
[Styling → GridLayout](/vue/components/styling/css-grid-layout/)), which
is the supported approach today.

| Variable | Default | Used for |

| `$grid-item-border-radius` | `12px` | The "use radius" class's border-radius — note that `GridItem`'s own `borderRadiusPx` prop is applied as an inline style and takes priority over this when `useBorderRadius` is set; see [GridItem props](/vue/components/grid-item/props/). |
| `$grid-item-text-color` | `white` | Reserved for item text color. |

## A genuine exception: `--grid-line-color`

Grid line guides (`showGridLines`) are **not** controlled by a SCSS
variable at all, despite an earlier version of this page claiming
otherwise as `$grid-line-color`. Checked directly against
`GridLayout.vue`'s own `<style>` block: the actual mechanism is a real
CSS custom property, set with an inline fallback:

```css
.grid::before {
  background-image: linear-gradient(to right, var(--grid-line-color, rgb(128 128 128 / 30%)) 1px, transparent 1px), ...;
}
```

Unlike every SCSS variable in the table above, `--grid-line-color`
**is** genuinely runtime-overridable from your own stylesheet, the same
way any CSS custom property is:

```css
.vue-grid-layout {
  --grid-line-color: #38bdf8;
}
```

Target the library's classes directly, after its stylesheet is loaded:

```css
/* After importing 'keystone-dashboard-layout-vue/style.css' */
.vue-grid-item.vue-static {
  background-color: #1e293b;
}
```

[Styling → GridLayout](/vue/components/styling/css-grid-layout/) for the

The internal event bus, from GridItem's own side.

The same shared event bus documented on
[GridLayout's eventbus events page](/vue/components/grid-layout/eventbus-events/) —
this page lists them from `GridItem`'s perspective: what it listens for,
and what it emits.

## Listens for (pushed down from GridLayout)

`changeDirection`, `compact`, `setBounded`, `setBorderRadiusPx`,
`setColNum`, `setDraggable`, `setEnableEditMode`, `setMargin`,
`setMaxRows`, `setResizable`, `setResizeHandles`, `setRowHeight`,
`setShowCloseButton`, `setTransformScale`, `setUseBorderRadius`,
`setUseCssTransforms`, `updateWidth` — each has a corresponding handler
registered on mount and deregistered on unmount.

The `setDraggable`/`setResizable`/`setBounded`/`setShowCloseButton`/
`setEnableEditMode`/`setUseBorderRadius`/`setBorderRadiusPx`/
`setResizeHandles` handlers only apply the pushed value when the item's
own matching prop is `null` — an explicit per-item prop always wins
over the cascade. `setUseCssTransforms` is the one exception: it applies
unconditionally, since there's no per-item override for it at all.

## Emits (reported up to GridLayout)

`dragEvent` and `resizeEvent`, both carrying an `IEventsData` payload —
emitted on every `dragstart`/`dragmove`/`dragend` (or
`resizestart`/`resizemove`/`resizeend`) tick. `itemClicked` (an
`IItemClickedData` payload) fires on a genuine click/tap, backing
`GridLayout`'s own `multiSelect` handling.

See [GridLayout's eventbus events](/vue/components/grid-layout/eventbus-events/)
for the full message table and payload shapes.

## Resize direction support

All four edges — top, right, bottom, left — and their diagonal corners
are resizable. Left/top-edge resizes move the item's position (`x`/`y`)
as well as its size, since growing from the left/top edge means the
opposite edge stays fixed. In RTL mode, this is mirrored correctly too —
dragging the right edge (rather than the left) is what moves the
anchor. See [Mirrored (RTL)](/vue/examples/mirrored-rtl/).

What keyboard and screen-reader support Keystone Dashboard Layout for Vue actually provides — and what it deliberately doesn't (yet).

Before keyboard support was added, there was no way to move or resize a
`GridItem` other than a mouse or touch drag. For a library whose entire
purpose is letting end users rearrange a layout, that's a real gap, not a
nice-to-have.

## What's implemented

### Keyboard move and resize

Every non-static, editable `GridItem` is keyboard-focusable
(`tabindex="0"`) and operable:

- **Arrow keys** move it by one grid unit, if it's draggable.
- **Shift + arrow keys** resize it by one grid unit, if it's resizable.

Each keypress is treated as a complete, atomic gesture — there's no
keyboard equivalent of a continuous drag to preview mid-way through —
and emits the same event pairs and eventBus messages the mouse-driven
path already uses, so compaction and collision handling apply
identically regardless of which input method triggered the change.

**Works with `multiSelect`'s group move/resize too** — arrow-key/
Shift+arrow movement on a focused, *selected* item moves/resizes every
other selected item by the same delta, the same as a mouse/touch drag
already does. See [Multi-select & group move/resize](/vue/examples/multi-select-group-move-resize/).

**Deliberately scoped to single-unit steps**, not a full
[WAI-ARIA grid](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/grid/) or
[application](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/) widget pattern
(roving `tabindex` between cells, a distinct "move mode" toggle key,
etc.). This library isn't a traditional data grid — it's a freeform
draggable canvas — so the full APG grid pattern doesn't map cleanly onto
it. The goal was closing the actual gap (no keyboard alternative existed
at all), not redesigning the interaction model.

### Screen reader support

- Each interactive item gets `role="group"` and
  `aria-roledescription="Draggable, resizable item"`, so a screen reader
  announces it as something other than a plain, silent `<div>`.
- `aria-describedby` points to a visually-hidden instructions string
  ("Press arrow keys to move." / "Press shift plus arrow keys to
  resize.", each only included if that action actually applies to the
  item) — discoverable on focus, not a mandatory upfront announcement.
- A visible focus outline, so a keyboard user can actually see which
  item currently has focus.

### A deliberate, non-obvious design decision worth calling out

Keyboard move/resize **ignores `dragAllowFrom`/`dragIgnoreFrom`/
`resizeIgnoreFrom`** entirely — those props restrict which DOM element a
*mouse* drag/resize gesture can originate from (see
[Drag allow/ignore elements](/vue/examples/drag-allow-ignore-elements/) and
[Custom drag handle](/vue/examples/custom-drag-handle-close-button/)),
which is a concept that doesn't map onto keyboard interaction at all —
there's no "which element did the keypress originate from" equivalent to
"which element did the mousedown originate from." A keyboard user who
focuses the item gets full move/resize access regardless of whether a
mouse user is restricted to a specific handle. This is intentional, not
an oversight: restricting keyboard users *further* than mouse users, just
because a mouse-specific UI affordance (a drag handle) exists, would be
the wrong direction for an accessibility feature to take.

### Localizable ARIA strings

The close button's label, `aria-roledescription`, and the keyboard
move/resize instructions are all overridable rather than hardcoded
English literals — see [Localizable ARIA strings](/vue/examples/aria-labels/).

## What's not covered (tracked, not silently ignored)

- **No roving-tabindex grid navigation.** Tabbing moves through items in
  DOM order (which usually, but not necessarily, matches visual order),
  the same as any other focusable elements on a page — there's no
  arrow-key-based "move focus to the item above/below/left/right"
  navigation independent of actually moving the focused item. That's part
  of the full APG grid pattern this deliberately doesn't implement.
- **No keyboard equivalent for the drag-from-outside / drag-between-grids
  examples** ([Drag, drop from outside](/vue/examples/outside-drag-drop/),
  [Drag, drop from grid to grid](/vue/examples/cross-grid-drag-drop/)) —
  those are consumer-level example code, not library internals, and
  would need their own keyboard handling written the same way the
  examples currently write their own mouse handling.
- **Not independently audited against WCAG success criteria** or run
  through an automated tool (axe, Lighthouse, etc.) — what's implemented
  was reasoned through manually against the specific gap found (no
  keyboard alternative), not verified against a full checklist. A real
  automated accessibility audit is a reasonable next step, and would
  likely find things this pass didn't.
- **Color contrast and the default item styling generally** haven't been
  reviewed — `GridItem`'s content is unstyled by default (see
  [Styling → GridItem](/vue/components/styling/css-grid-item/)), so this
  is mostly a consumer responsibility, but the library's own default
  close button and focus outline colors haven't been explicitly checked
  against contrast ratios.

## Verifying this

The component test suite's own "keyboard accessibility" tests cover:
focus attributes present/absent correctly based on static/edit-mode
state, arrow-key movement (including bounds clamping and the
`isDraggable: false` guard), shift+arrow resize (including `minW`/`minH`
clamping and the `isResizable: false` guard), and that non-arrow keys and
disabled edit-mode are correctly no-ops. See [Production readiness](/vue/guide/project/production-readiness/)
for the current test-suite numbers.

The map worth knowing before digging deeper into how the library is
built — `GridLayout` and `GridItem` carry almost the entire
implementation, and their relationship isn't obvious from reading either
file in isolation.

## Two entry points

The main package entry (`GridLayout`, `GridItem`, and everything that
needs a live component instance or DOM) is one thing; a separate
`/core` subpath export is the pure grid-layout math those components are
built on — collision detection, compaction, movement, alignment guides,
breakpoint resolution, serialization, and validation — with zero Vue
dependency and no live DOM required. Useful standalone, e.g. for
validating a layout server-side.

`/core` ships as its own build (`es`/`cjs` only), separate from the main
library's build (which still needs a UMD output for script-tag/CDN
consumers, and Vite doesn't support multiple entry points when `umd` is
one of the output formats).

## Pluggable compaction

Every compaction call (drag end, resize end, mount, breakpoint change,
`compactNow()`) routes through one internal helper, which checks the
`compactor` prop first, falling back to whichever of the five built-in
strategies `compactType` selects. `compactor: null` (the default) means
"use whichever built-in strategy `compactType` selects" — a purely
additive override, not a replacement for that prop. All five built-in
strategies are exported from both the main entry and `/core`, as a
starting point for writing a custom one. See [Pluggable compaction](/vue/examples/pluggable-compaction/).

## Undo/redo

Opt-in, snapshot-at-committed-change granularity, not per intermediate
drag-move frame. The pre-mutation layout is captured explicitly at
`dragstart`/`resizestart` and committed at `dragend`/`resizeend` — after
the position update and compaction have already run — rather than
reading a single shared "last known state" implicitly at commit time,
which would only ever see "nothing's changed yet" if read too early in
the gesture. See [Undo/redo](/vue/examples/undo-redo/).

## How GridLayout and GridItem talk to each other

A consumer renders `GridItem`s themselves, inside `GridLayout`'s default
slot — `GridLayout` doesn't create your items for you. It creates
exactly one extra, hidden `GridItem` internally: the drag placeholder
shown while dragging or resizing.

Communication runs two ways:

### `$parent`

`GridItem` reads its parent instance directly, which works because it's
always rendered as a direct child of `GridLayout`'s template. This is a
**one-time snapshot at mount**, not a live reactive reference — a later
change to a `GridLayout` prop won't be reflected through this path no
matter how many times it's read. Anything that needs to reach an
already-mounted `GridItem` after the fact uses the eventBus below
instead.

### The eventBus

`GridLayout` provides an event emitter that every `GridItem` injects —
the direction for `GridLayout` pushing targeted updates down to
potentially many items at once (rather than re-rendering every item on
every relevant change), and for items reporting drag/resize activity
back up. Cascading settings like `isDraggable`/`isResizable`/`isBounded`/
`showCloseButton` propagate this way — each only applied by an item
whose own prop is left at its inherit-from-parent default.

## Inside GridItem: composable split

`GridItem`'s own drag, resize, and keyboard-interaction logic each live
in their own composable rather than one large file — genuinely coupled
(drag/resize act on the same DOM element via the same native
pointer-driven engine; keyboard deliberately reuses drag/resize's own
resolved state and event paths, so the same collision/compaction
handling already tested against the mouse path applies to keyboard
input with no separate handling needed on `GridLayout`'s side at all),
but each still gets its own file, name, and test surface.

## Native drag/resize engine

Both drag and resize wire up a native, Pointer Events-based engine once
per `GridItem` — no third-party drag/resize library at all. Unlike an
approach that needs re-invoking on every relevant prop/state change to
reconfigure, this engine reads its own current options fresh on every
`pointerdown`, so the wiring only needs to happen once. Each gesture is
guarded to one pointer at a time per element, so a second concurrent
pointer (two fingers, an accidental palm touch mid-drag) can't silently
hijack tracking.

## Cross-grid drag/drop

`allowCrossGridDrag` needs separate `GridLayout` instances — frequently
with no Vue ancestor/descendant relationship to each other at all — to
find one another. A plain, module-level registry (not Vue reactive
state, not provide/inject) is the answer: every participating grid
registers itself on mount and deregisters on unmount; the only lookup
either side needs is a scan over whatever's currently registered, fine
at the scale this feature operates at. See [Drag, drop from grid to grid](/vue/examples/cross-grid-drag-drop/).

## Outside drag/drop

Architecturally the simplest of the three drag-related features, since
it's the only one that never needs to coordinate with anything else — a
grid with `allowOutsideDrop` set only cares about drags happening
directly over its own root element, from a source it has no ongoing
relationship with before or after the drop. Reuses the same
placeholder/dragging state a normal in-grid drag already drives, rather
than a second, parallel preview mechanism. See [Drag, drop from outside](/vue/examples/outside-drag-drop/).

## Responsive breakpoints and alignment guides

The per-breakpoint layout cache, the currently active breakpoint, and
the function that finds or generates the right layout for the current
container width all live together, since the coupling there is narrow.
Alignment guides are simpler still — a pure function (given the active
item's live position/size and the rest of the layout, returns which
edges align) called from the existing drag/resize hook points, not a
separate composable or watcher of its own.

## Testing implications

`GridLayout` and `GridItem` are tested together, mounting a real
`GridLayout` with real `GridItem` children in its slot — the only way to
exercise the `$parent`/eventBus contract the way production actually
uses it. Testing `GridItem` with a hand-rolled fake parent would
validate a contract that might not match what `GridLayout` actually
provides. See [Testing philosophy](/vue/guide/project/testing/) for the fuller picture.

## Scope

This compares projects in the same category as this library —
**draggable/resizable dashboard layout engines** (position arbitrary
widgets on a grid, drag/resize them, responsive breakpoints) — not data
tables/grids (Kendo's Grid, AG Grid, etc.), which solve a different
problem. For commercial layout-engine peers, see
[Comparison: commercial](/vue/guide/project/comparison-commercial/) instead.

Projects compared: **`vue-grid-layout`** (jbaysolutions, the original
Vue library this space descends from), **`grid-layout-plus`** (a Vue 3
migration of the original, now the closest thing to a de-facto default
by real npm download volume), **`react-grid-layout`** (the React
equivalent this whole category traces back to, recently rewritten with
a hooks-based v2), and **`gridstack.js`** (framework-agnostic, ships
official Vue/React/Angular wrappers).

## The headline finding

The most-starred Vue option, `vue-grid-layout`, still has no official
Vue 3 release years after Vue 3 shipped — its own issue tracker confirms
people were still asking about a Vue 3 alternative well after Vue 3's
release. What filled the gap instead is a scatter of independently
maintained community forks with no single obvious default among
them — except that one of them, `grid-layout-plus`, has actually
emerged as something close to a de-facto default by real usage: an
order of magnitude more weekly downloads than the other forks, its own
polished documentation site, and a regular release history. It's a
faithful Vue 3 port of the original codebase, not an expanded fork — its
own feature set matches the original almost exactly, nothing more.

## Where this project genuinely leads

Cross-referencing the table above, the features with **no equivalent in
any alternative checked**: magnetic snap-to-grid (distinct from a
visual guide), visual alignment guides, the blocked-move feedback
event, named layout presets, grid-to-SVG export, localizable ARIA
strings as a dedicated prop surface, live-resyncing per-item
`autoHeight`, and multi-select with group move/resize. None of these
are exotic — they're the kind of real-world friction points (hand-rolled
persistence, a hand-wired collision-shake animation, English-only
screen reader text) a dedicated roadmap process exists specifically to
find and close one at a time.

## Where this project is genuinely behind

- **Ecosystem size and battle-testing.** `react-grid-layout` and
  `gridstack.js` have years more production usage across far more
  companies — not a feature gap this library can close by writing code,
  just a newer project.
- **Framework breadth.** `gridstack.js` covers Vue, React, and Angular
  from one core engine. This library is Vue-only by design today — a
  reasonable scope choice, but a real limitation for a team needing the
  same layout logic across multiple frameworks (see the
  [landing page](/)'s own React/Angular framework picker for where that's headed).
- **Sub-grids / nesting.** `gridstack.js` supports grids-within-grids as
  first-class nested structures. This library's cross-grid feature is
  sibling-to-sibling dragging between independent grid instances — a
  different capability, not a nesting system.
- **Swap-on-drag.** In `gridstack.js`'s default top-gravity mode,
  dragging one item onto another of the same size swaps their
  positions. This library only pushes items aside via compaction — an
  item landing on another never swaps with it.
- **A specific, unusually feature-rich fork** (`@marsio/vue-grid-layout`,
  minimal current adoption but technically ambitious) offers multiple
  persistence backends and a worker-based layout engine for very large
  layouts, neither of which this project has yet (both are on the
  [Roadmap](/vue/guide/project/roadmap/)). It does **not**, however,
  have an equivalent to several things this project already checked and
  confirmed it does have, contrary to an earlier version of this
  comparison: align/distribute commands over a multi-selection
  (`alignSelected`/`distributeSelected`, exposed on the `GridLayout`
  instance), a configurable resize-handle *set* (`resizeHandles`,
  restricting which specific corners/edges render, not just an
  all-or-nothing toggle), and spacing guides with distance labels
  (`showSpacingGuides`). The fork in turn has no equivalent to this
  project's cross-grid drag, outside-drop typed-payload helper, or
  multi-select **group resize** specifically (its own docs note group
  move is supported but group resize is not).

## Bottom line

For a Vue 3, TypeScript-first dashboard layout library, the realistic
field is small and genuinely fragmented — the most-starred option still
doesn't officially support Vue 3, and what exists instead is a handful
of differently-maintained community forks with no clear default.
Measured against that actual field, this project has meaningfully more
features (several with no equivalent in any alternative checked) and a
more rigorously documented test/coverage process, at the cost of being
a newer, smaller-community project without the multi-year production
track record the category's oldest entries can claim.
How Keystone Dashboard Layout for Vue compares to Kendo TileLayout and DevExtreme's Dashboard Designer.

## Scope, and why this is separate from Comparison: alternatives

[Comparison: alternatives](/vue/guide/project/comparison-alternatives/)
scopes itself to open-source peers in the same category. This page
covers two commercial products instead, kept separate since both the
licensing model and (for one of the two) the actual product category
differ enough that folding them into the same table would be
misleading.

Two things worth correcting up front: Kendo's actual component is
called **TileLayout** (available for jQuery, Angular, React, and
Blazor) — "DashboardLayout" isn't a real Kendo product name. And
DevExtreme's **Dashboard Designer** is a full BI platform, not a
standalone layout component — it bundles data source binding,
drill-down interactivity, a WYSIWYG designer, and export around its own
layout mechanism. This page compares against just its layout engine
(the drag/resize/arrange mechanics), since that's the only part in the
same category as this library.

## The bigger architectural difference

Both commercial products use a **recursive binary split-pane tree**:
adding a new item splits the largest existing pane in half; resizing
means dragging the separator line between two adjacent panes, not
independent per-item resize handles — the same model as a tiling window
manager or an IDE's split editor panes. This library uses **freeform,
independent `x`/`y`/`w`/`h` grid coordinates** instead: any item can
move to any free position on its own, with its own resize handles on
its own edges.

This isn't a minor detail — several rows below aren't simple
"missing feature" gaps, they're different tradeoffs a different
architecture makes. A split-pane tree structurally guarantees no
overlaps and no compaction step, at the cost of items never being fully
independent of their neighbors. Freeform coordinates give full
independent placement, at the cost of needing an explicit
collision/compaction system. Neither is strictly better; they suit
different products.

## Feature comparison

| Feature | This project | Kendo TileLayout | DevExtreme Dashboard (layout engine) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Layout model | Freeform x/y/w/h grid coordinates | CSS Grid, col/row/colSpan/rowSpan | Recursive binary split-pane tree |
| Resize any of 8 edges/corners independently | Yes | No — bottom/right edges + bottom-right corner only | No — drag the separator between two adjacent panes |
| Drag to an arbitrary free position | Yes | No — reorders within CSS Grid auto-flow | No — inserts into the tree at a new split point |
| Click-to-select, click-to-place reorder (no drag gesture) | No | **Yes** — a real, non-drag accessibility alternative worth considering here | No |
| Vue support | Native, ground-up | **None** — jQuery, Angular, React, Blazor only | Via a wrapper layer over a shared core |
| Licensing | MIT, free | Commercial, but free for the React build specifically | Commercial, no free tier |
| Cross-grid drag/drop between independent instances | Yes | No | No |
| Drag-and-drop from outside the component | Yes | No | No — Toolbox is click-to-add, not a drag gesture |
| Responsive breakpoints | Yes | No | Auto-stretches to fit its container — a different, non-breakpoint mechanism |
| Undo/redo | Yes | No | No — dashboard-level save/reload only |
| Multi-select group move/resize | Yes | No | No — single-item drag only |
| Magnetic snap-to-grid / alignment guides | Yes (both) | No | No |
| Keyboard move/resize | Yes | Comparable, via Ctrl+arrow (resize) / Shift+arrow (reorder) | Not documented as a distinct mode |
| Per-item lock against rearrangement | Yes (`isStatic`) | Yes | Closer to a dashboard-level view mode than a per-item flag |
| **Maximize/restore an item to fill the surface** | **No — a real, confirmed gap** | No | **Yes** |
| Save/restore layout state | Yes | Yes — comparable | Yes — comparable |
| Export layout as image/SVG | Yes, dependency-free | No | Yes, but exports the dashboard's data visualizations, not a plain layout-shell export |
| Data source binding, drill-down, BI charting | **Out of scope entirely — a deliberate boundary** | No (presentation-only, same category as this library) | **Yes — its entire reason to exist** |

## Honest summary

Against **Kendo TileLayout**: this library is ahead on nearly every
drag/resize/layout-mechanics dimension — full 8-edge independent resize
vs. a 3-handle/axis-restricted model, freeform positioning vs.
reorder-only, cross-grid drag, outside drop, snap/alignment guides,
undo/redo, multi-select. TileLayout's genuine advantages: being one
component in a large commercial suite with paid support, a mature
click-move-click accessibility mode this library doesn't have, and
(for the React build specifically) being free. There's no Vue build to
compare against directly at all.

Against **DevExtreme Dashboard**: these aren't real competitors for
most consumers — Dashboard Designer is a BI-authoring product where
drag/resize layout is one supporting piece of a much larger
data-analytics platform, not something you'd choose *for* its layout
engine alone. The one genuine, worth-tracking gap even at the pure
layout-mechanics level is **maximize/restore** — a common, useful
dashboard pattern this library doesn't have. It's tracked on the
[Roadmap](/vue/guide/project/roadmap/), not yet designed.

## What's not worth chasing from either

- **Kendo's CSS Grid-based, resize-restricted-to-3-handles model** —
  adopting this would be a regression, not a gap to close.
- **DevExtreme's recursive split-pane structure itself** — rebuilding
  around that architecture would abandon the freeform positioning model
  that's core to what this library is. If a split-pane mode is ever
  genuinely wanted, it belongs as an alternative, opt-in mode, not a
  replacement.
- **DevExtreme's BI/data-analytics layer entirely** — a different
  product category by design, not a scope this library is trying to
  grow into.

## Security

Zero runtime dependencies is the strongest possible position on third-party runtime-dependency risk here. No `eval`/dynamic code execution anywhere in the library's own source. No telemetry, analytics, or network calls of any kind.

## Browser/runtime support
